title: Congenital Defects of the Cardiovascular System

paragraphs.text: 76 Congenital Defects of the Cardiovascular System
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Congenital heart defects are the most common type of birth defects worldwide. The following chapter provides an overview of the anatomy, physiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, and management strategies for a wide range of congenital heart disease in neonates and infants. Although the information herein is detailed, it is important to keep in mind that many different anatomic and physiologic variants are encountered in practice, often altering clinical management. The chapter is generally organized based on the predominant pathophysiology—cyanotic, obstructive, or shunting—for a given congenital heart defect. There can be considerable overlap between these physiologies, particularly in complex forms of congenital heart disease involving multiple defects. Defect physiology can also change considerably over time, particularly in the immediate postnatal transitional period around ductal closure. Prompt recognition and diagnosis of hemodynamically significant congenital heart defects can greatly impact effective management and outcomes in affected newborns and infants.
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: In dextro-transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA), the aorta arises from the right ventricle, which receives systemic venous deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle, which receives pulmonary venous oxygenated blood. The blood flow in these patients is in parallel with the deoxygenated blood entering the aorta and recirculating to the body, while the richly oxygenated pulmonary venous return is recirculated to the lungs. In the absence of any shunting across connections between the systemic and pulmonary circulations to allow mixing of the deoxygenated and oxygenated blood, it results in systemic hypoxia and is often lethal. In D-TGA, three levels where
paragraphs.heading: Dextro-Transposition of the Great Arteries Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: mixing can occur are atrial level defect (patent foramen ovale [PFO] or atrial septal defect [ASD]), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), or ventricular septal defect (VSD). The most effective site of mixing is at the atrial level through a PFO or ASD, with the other forms (PDA and VSD) being less reliable. It is therefore extremely important at birth to make sure that there is an adequately sized atrial level communication.
paragraphs.heading: Dextro-Transposition of the Great Arteries Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Associated defects have a dramatic effect on the presentation and pathophysiology of newborn infants with D-TGA. At a minimum, an atrial level defect with balanced bidirectional shunting is essential for survival. The presence of a PDA also allows for additional shunting from the aorta (deoxygenated blood) to the pulmonary artery (oxygenated blood), resulting in increased pulmonary venous return and added left-to-right shunting at the atrial level. An associated VSD occurs in about 25% of infants with D-TGA. Its presence contributes to mixing of the oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood, but, as previously stated, atrial level mixing is the most reliable. Coarctation of the aorta or aortic arch interruption can also occur in association with D-TGA, particularly in cases with a subpulmonary VSD.1
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: D-TGA is the most common cyanotic heart defect identified in the first week of life, and the diagnosis should be considered in any cyanotic neonate. Fetal diagnosis is common, and factors such as hypermobility of the atrial septum and reversal of diastolic flow in the PDA on fetal echocardiography can potentially predict the need for urgent balloon atrial septostomy.2 Even with prenatal diagnosis, however, profound hypoxia caused by a highly restrictive atrial level defect can lead to rapid deterioration and death within the first hours of life. Respiratory symptoms in this disorder are absent or limited to hyperpnea or tachypnea. The patient’s second heart sound is loud and single because of the anterior position of the aorta and
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: the posterior position of the pulmonary artery. A holosystolic murmur, when present, suggests an associated VSD; a systolic ejection murmur is auscultated in the setting of pulmonary stenosis (PS). In the absence of these associated defects, murmurs are generally not heard. The peripheral pulses are normal unless coarctation of the aorta is present. Persistent ductal patency or high pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) will affect the clinical findings of an associated VSD or coarctation of the aorta with potential for reverse differential cyanosis showing preductal saturation in the upper extremities lower than postductal saturation in the lower extremities.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is usually normal or may demonstrate right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy after a few weeks of life. Similarly, the classic egg-shaped heart with increased pulmonary vascularity on the chest radiograph might not be seen in the newborn period. Echocardiography defines the diagnosis, associated defects, and coronary artery anatomy, which are central to surgical planning.3 Cardiac catheterization is usually reserved for neonates requiring balloon atrial septostomy, and it is occasionally useful for further delineating other anatomic details, although it is rarely necessary to evaluate the coronary arteries (Fig. 76.1). Dual-source computed tomography angiography (CTA) can also be used for delineating coronary artery origin and course, as well as other associated intra- and extracardiac anomalies.4
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Maintaining patency of the ductus arteriosus with intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion in newborn infants with D-TGA often improves arterial oxygenation by increasing shunting from the oxygen-rich pulmonary artery to the deoxygenated aorta. Aortic to pulmonary artery shunting at the ductal level may increase pulmonary venous return, distending the left atrium and facilitating left-to-right
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: atrial shunting of fully oxygenated blood. If the prostaglandin E1 infusion does not result in adequate systemic oxygenation, the atrial level defect is enlarged by balloon atrial septostomy performed either at the bedside or in the cardiac catheterization lab under echocardiographic guidance.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Historically, the surgical interventions for D-TGA were the atrial switch operations, Senning (1959) and Mustard (1964). In these procedures, deoxygenated blood from the vena cavae is baffled to the morphologic left ventricle and then to the pulmonary artery, while the oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is directed to the morphologic right ventricle and the aorta. This results in physiologic circulation. However, the Senning and Mustard procedures are associated with a number of long-term complications, including RV dysfunction, systemic venous baffle obstruction and leaks, and atrial arrhythmias, as well as increased right atrial volumes and decreased right atrial emptying fractions.5
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Drs. Adib Jatene and Magdi Yacoub pioneered the anatomic repair of D-TGA via the arterial switch operation, which requires transection of the aorta and main pulmonary artery, reconnection to establish ventriculoarterial concordance (systemic left ventricle to the aorta and pulmonic right ventricle to the main pulmonary artery), and reimplantation of the coronary arteries to the neoaortic root. Other associated intracardiac defects are generally repaired at the time of the initial surgery. The arterial switch operation is optimally performed in the first week of life for infants with D-TGA. If there is a prolonged delay, the risk of left ventricular (LV) deconditioning and resultant inability to function adequately as the systemic ventricle increases. Long-term follow-up data on patients who have undergone the arterial switch operation are quite favorable.7 Risk factors for early mortality include prematurity, low birth weight, and RV hypoplasia. Abnormal coronary artery anatomy (particularly in cases with an intramural course), a risk factor in earlier experiences, can now be managed effectively, although with potentially higher hospital morbidity.6 Long-term follow-up studies demonstrate excellent ventricular function, normal rhythm, and low incidence of obstruction at the aortic and coronary suture lines. Narrowing in the supravalvar pulmonary area and branch pulmonary arteries may require subsequent surgeries or catheter interventions. Neoaortic root dilation and neoaortic valve regurgitation are found in some children, but these rarely require further intervention in childhood. Progressive neoaortic regurgitation requiring neoaortic valve replacement remains a long-term complication in adulthood.7 Follow-up data in children 16 years of age with D-TGA from the Boston Circulatory Arrest Study suggest that adolescents with D-TGA who have undergone the arterial switch operation are at increased
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: neurodevelopmental risk and may benefit (along with other children born with congenital heart disease) from ongoing surveillance to identify emerging difficulties.8
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In 1888, Etienne Fallot described the association of a large VSD, infundibular (subvalvar) and valvar PS, RV hypertrophy, and a large aorta overriding the ventricular septum—the tetralogy which bears his name. The spectrum of pulmonary lesions in tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) can range from mild PS with adequate oxygen saturation to pulmonary atresia with very low oxygen saturations. Infants with severe PS or atresia may have severely hypoplastic, discontinuous, or absent pulmonary arteries, with major aortopulmonary (AP) collateral arteries serving as the primary source of pulmonary blood flow. In TOF, cyanosis is proportional to the degree of right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction, with severe obstruction limiting pulmonary blood flow and leading to very low saturation. Shunting across the VSD is determined by an intricate balance between the systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). Hypercyanotic spells arise from acute worsening of RVOT narrowing or stenosis from the release of endogenous catecholamines, such as seen with agitation in a dehydrated infant, leading to increased PVR more than SVR, resulting in right-to-left shunting and worsening systemic desaturations.9
paragraphs.heading: Tetralogy of Fallot Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: A right aortic arch is found in approximately 25% of patients with TOF.10 Coronary artery anomalies (e.g., left anterior descending coronary artery arising from the right coronary artery) are not uncommon and must be identified prior to surgical intervention.11 The branch pulmonary arteries may be stenotic or discontinuous with collateral supply from the aorta. Some patients also have multiple VSDs or ASDs, anomalous systemic venous drainage, or atrioventricular valve abnormalities. A rare, complex form is TOF with absent pulmonary valve, which results in pulmonary valve annulus hypoplasia, severe branch pulmonary artery dilation, significant bronchial compression, and airway abnormalities, including bronchomalacia.9 Up to 25% have associated chromosomal abnormalities with the most common being trisomy 21, 22q11.2 deletion, trisomy 18, and trisomy 13.12
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of TOF is directly related to the severity of RVOT obstruction. The intensely cyanotic newborn generally has severe PS or atresia with markedly diminished pulmonary blood flow and right-to-left shunting across the VSD. The minimally cyanotic or acyanotic infant
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: has a lesser degree of PS with mainly left-to-right shunting across the VSD. On exam, in neonates with TOF, the primary murmur is a systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border secondary to PS/RVOT obstruction. There may also be a single second heart sound due to marked decrease of its pulmonary component and a palpable RV impulse. The VSD in TOF is generally large and unrestrictive and does not produce a significant murmur. A continuous murmur may suggest systemic-to-pulmonary collaterals as the source of pulmonary blood flow.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: In the newborn with TOF, the classic finding on chest X-ray is a boot-shaped heart caused by RV hypertrophy and consequent upturned cardiac apex. The pulmonary vascular markings should also be carefully examined and may reflect the severity of RVOT obstruction. Echocardiography is the primary diagnostic tool and illustrates the anterior malalignment VSD resulting from anterior displacement of the conal septum leading to variable degrees of RVOT obstruction, RV hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta (Fig. 76.2). The levels and degrees of pulmonary obstruction and the size of the main and branch pulmonary arteries should be delineated, as well as other associated abnormalities, including coronary artery anomalies, additional VSDs, or collateral vessels.13 Presurgical diagnostic cardiac catheterization is only indicated if the pulmonary artery anatomy and pulmonary blood flow sources cannot be defined by noninvasive imaging modalities.14
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Neonates with severe cyanosis in the immediate postnatal period are stabilized via intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus and increase pulmonary blood flow. In general, these neonates require a palliative systemic-to-pulmonary shunt (e.g., Blalock-Thomas-Taussig or central shunt) or complete
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: repair in the newborn period to provide a reliable source of pulmonary blood flow. Balloon dilation or stenting of the stenotic pulmonary valve or RVOT has been favored in a few centers as an alternative to shunts.15 Stenting of the ductus arteriosus is another approach to providing stable pulmonary blood flow.16 Rehabilitation of branch pulmonary artery stenosis by surgery or interventional catheterization is another important step at the time of primary repair or as part of a staged approach. This is of particular importance in patients with pulmonary atresia and major AP collaterals.17
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Complete TOF repair consists of relief of PS and RVOT obstruction (often with a transannular patch) and patch closure of the VSD. Associated intracardiac defects such as atrial level shunts are also addressed. In the absence of marked pulmonary artery hypoplasia or unfavorable coronary artery anatomy, surgery can be undertaken at virtually any age, with most centers doing elective repairs between 4 and 6 months of age. Neonatal TOF repair is feasible in the setting of normal or appropriate pulmonary artery size at birth.18
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In tricuspid atresia (TA), platelike tissue replaces the tricuspid valve, resulting in no direct communication between the right atrium and right ventricle. Systemic venous return from the vena cavae enters the right atrium and crosses the atrial septum with resultant complete mixing of the systemic and pulmonary venous return in the left atrium. Pulmonary blood flow is supplied by left-to-right shunting through either a PDA or VSD. Associated RV hypoplasia and pulmonary artery hypoplasia are proportional to the size of the VSD and the degree of subpulmonary stenosis and PS. The degree of hypoxemia is proportional to the relative systemic and pulmonary blood flows. Neonates with TA, a small VSD, and severe PS have severely limited pulmonary blood flow and are ductal dependent. Those with a large VSD and no PS have unrestrictive pulmonary blood flow, and, as the PVR falls, pulmonary blood flow dramatically increases with resultant signs and symptoms of pulmonary overcirculation, including feeding difficulties and growth failure.
paragraphs.heading: Tricuspid Atresia Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: All neonates with TA must have an atrial level defect for postnatal survival. Other associated lesions include VSD, TGA, atrioventricular septal defect, and aortic coarctation. The VSD size is extremely important in neonates with TA and TGA, as oxygenated blood flows through the VSD into the right ventricle and then the aorta. Restriction of blood flow through the VSD can compromise flow to the aorta and the systemic circulation.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: The typical neonatal presentation of TA is cyanosis at or before ductal closure in an infant with a murmur. Precordial activity is normal, and the second heart sound is often
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: single. There may be a systolic ejection murmur if there is RVOT obstruction. If the VSD is large, tachypnea, a LV impulse, and a third heart sound may develop during the first few days of life as the PVR falls. Hepatic enlargement is an indicator of a restrictive ASD and elevated right atrial pressures.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The ECG is usually diagnostic in neonates with TA, demonstrating right atrial enlargement and left-axis deviation. The chest radiograph tends to be nonspecific, although in severely cyanotic neonates it may show decreased pulmonary vascularity. The echocardiogram (Fig. 76.3) clearly defines the anatomy, in addition to abnormalities of the great arteries or aortic coarctation. Diagnosis as well as associated anatomical defects can be accurately identified prenatally by fetal echocardiography.19 Heart catheterization may be performed for balloon atrial septostomy in those with a restrictive atrial septum.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Flow across the VSD to supply the pulmonary circulation may be adequate in the first months of life as long as the atrial level defect remains unrestrictive. It is generally possible to predict by echocardiogram when infants require a PDA to maintain adequate arterial saturations. A balloon atrial septostomy is rarely necessary unless there is significant restriction at the atrial level. Off bypass surgical septostomy on the beating heart has been used in rare cases.20 If a newborn is deemed ductal dependent or if hypoxia increases in the first month of life, a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt is necessary to provide adequate pulmonary blood flow and oxygenation. Conversion to a bidirectional cavopulmonary (Glenn shunt) anastomosis is usually considered between 3 and 6 months of age. Some infants with well-balanced systemic and pulmonary flows can proceed directly to an early bidirectional Glenn operation followed by a total cavopulmonary (Fontan operation) connection at about 2 to 3 years of age.21 Although nearly 10% of children will not reach Fontan completion, among children who undergo the Fontan type of operation those with TA have an excellent long-term prognosis, with a low prevalence of ventricular dysfunction, mitral regurgitation, arrhythmias, and systemic venous congestion.22
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: The pulmonary valve in pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (PA/IVS) can range from a well-formed pulmonary annulus with a plate or membrane that obstructs outflow to a completely underdeveloped valve. All forms may lead to severe RV hypertrophy, RV dysfunction, and variable degrees of RV hypoplasia. Because the ventricular septum is intact, pulmonary blood flow in PA/IVS is ductal dependent and can only occur via shunting at the level of the atria and PDA. The tricuspid valve is often abnormal in
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Atresia With Intact Ventricular Septum Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: patients with PA/IVS, ranging from a dysplastic appearance, variable hypoplasia, stenosis, and regurgitation.
paragraphs.heading: Pulmonary Atresia With Intact Ventricular Septum Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: A very important prognostic feature in PA/IVS concerns the presence or absence of ventriculocoronary connections (sinusoids and fistulae) and coronary artery abnormalities. These must be well defined prior to surgical or transcatheter intervention. In the case of RV-dependent coronary circulation, where coronary artery flow depends on high RV pressures for adequate myocardial perfusion, decompressing the RV can lead to untoward consequences such as myocardial ischemia, infarction, and death. Its presence is also associated with high early mortality in those patients undergoing single-ventricle palliation.23
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: Fetal diagnosis of PA/IVS frequently identifies risk factors for subsequent transcatheter and surgical management, including tricuspid valve and RV hypoplasia, coronary sinusoids, and fistulae.24 Neonates with PA/IVS develop severe hypoxemia as the ductus arteriosus closes and can rapidly become unstable with tachypnea, tachycardia, hepatomegaly, and cardiorespiratory collapse. Cyanosis becomes apparent within hours of birth and is progressive. Tachypnea may be prominent. First and second heart sounds are single, and there may be a holosystolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border consistent with tricuspid regurgitation. A PDA murmur may be audible, particularly following initiation of prostaglandin infusion. Unless there is severe tricuspid regurgitation or a restrictive atrial communication,
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: the liver generally is not enlarged while ductal patency is maintained.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Chest radiography in PA/IVS often shows cardiomegaly due to right atrial enlargement. Echocardiography is diagnostic, demonstrating the pulmonary valve atresia, tricuspid valve abnormalities, degree of RV hypoplasia, and coronary anomalies, including sinusoids and findings suggestive of coronary fistulae. Cardiac catheterization is indicated to assess coronary flow, the presence (including size and location) or absence of coronary sinusoids and fistulae, and pulmonary blood flow sources, as well as for consideration of pulmonary valve intervention.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion is essential for maintaining ductal patency in PA/IVS. Careful assessment of the anatomy and physiology provides a framework for transcatheter consideration and surgical management.25 Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty is feasible in infants with even a diminutive pulmonary valve orifice, and other transcatheter techniques, including radiofrequency perforation of the valve, may be considered. Although still in the early experience and offered at only a few centers, fetal intervention to perforate the pulmonary valve can allow for future biventricular repair in patients who otherwise would have been univentricular repair candidates. Perventricular pulmonary valve perforation has also allowed for successful RV decompression.26
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: If interventional catheterization is unsuccessful, surgical valvotomy can be performed unless RV-dependent coronary circulation is present. In these circumstances, RV decompression can result in coronary hypoperfusion; therefore a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt is recommended as initial palliation to provide pulmonary blood flow. In infants who have undergone successful surgical or transcatheter valvotomies, RV growth is possible and biventricular circulation can be restored. Severe tricuspid and RV hypoplasia or RVdependent coronary circulation are indications for single ventricle palliation.25 Infants with RV hypoplasia should also be considered candidates for superior cavopulmonary (Glenn) anastomosis combined with closure of the atrial level defect (the so-called 1.5 ventricle repair). This results in a direction of inferior vena cava flow across the tricuspid valve into the RV, promoting potential RV growth.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve, there is arrested delamination of the leaflets during valve development. In particular, the septal leaflet can become tethered to the interventricular septum to varying degrees with apical displacement of its annular attachment, potentially leading to significant tricuspid regurgitation. The anterior tricuspid leaflet can also become markedly enlarged and redundant (“sail-like”), causing RVOT obstruction with decreased
paragraphs.heading: Ebstein Anomaly Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: pulmonary blood flow and functional or anatomic pulmonary atresia. Secondary to apical tricuspid annular displacement into the right ventricle, a portion of the RV becomes atrialized, detrimentally affecting its contractile efficiency.27 Forward pulmonary blood flow is therefore dependent on the severity of tricuspid valve displacement and regurgitation and RV atrialization and dysfunction. If functional or anatomic pulmonary atresia occurs, an obligatory right-toleft shunt must exist at the atrial level, and its degree is proportional to the severity of the tricuspid valve abnormality.28
paragraphs.heading: Ebstein Anomaly Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Patients with Ebstein anomaly often have other associated intracardiac lesions, including the aforementioned pulmonary atresia and atrial level defects. Conduction system abnormalities such as accessory pathways (e.g., Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) are found in up to 20% of cases.28
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: Infants with severe Ebstein anomaly may present with profound cyanosis, tachypnea, and cardiovascular collapse. Cyanosis is dependent on the extent of atrial right-to-left shunting. A low-frequency holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation is often heard, and the first heart sound may be widely split.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The ECG of infants with severe Ebstein anomaly often shows an rSr′ pattern in the right precordial leads, suggesting RV dilation. Chest radiography can demonstrate severe cardiomegaly caused by right atrial dilation. Echocardiography helps delineate the extent of tricuspid valve displacement, atrial level shunting, and functional or anatomic pulmonary atresia. The ratio of the right atrial plus atrialized RV size to the functional RV plus left heart (left atrium and ventricle) size has been utilized as a measure of severity and outcome. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows for volumetric and functional measurements of the right ventricle, and serial assessments can be used for monitoring of disease progression.29
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Mild forms of Ebstein anomaly require no specific treatment early on, and infants in general do well. The severely affected neonate with severe tricuspid valve apical displacement and regurgitation is often ductal dependent with minimal or no anterograde flow across the pulmonary valve.28 Maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandin E1 infusion can be useful in the short term; however, ductal flow into the pulmonary artery can make antegrade flow more difficult. In severe Ebstein anomaly, measures to lower the PVR, including nitric oxide, and attempts to wean prostaglandin E1 might be necessary before anterograde flow across the pulmonary valve can be established. Brief support with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation to facilitate fetal-to-neonatal transition has been successful in limited cases. Surgical repair or replacement of the valve is feasible and may be indicated
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: in older children, but it is not useful in neonates. Either transplantation or surgical exclusion of the right ventricle, with plans for a long-term, single-ventricle palliation might be the only alternatives for the neonate with severe Ebstein anomaly and persistent cyanosis.30
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection or return (TAPVC/TAPVR) comprises a group of defects in which all of the pulmonary veins carrying oxygenated blood drain into the systemic venous circulation rather than normally to the left atrium. A number of distinct variants have been identified:
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Supracardiac type—In its most common form, an ascending
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: vertical vein emanates from the pulmonary venous confluence posterior to the left atrium and connects to the left innominate vein, which then drains to the superior vena cava (SVC) and right atrium. Infracardiac type—A descending vertical vein emanates from
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: the pulmonary venous confluence posterior to the left atrium and courses inferiorly, crossing through the diaphragm and the liver with variable drainage to the ductus venosus, hepatic veins, portal vein, or inferior vena cava with obstruction at one or more of these sites and eventual pulmonary venous drainage to the right atrium. Cardiac type—Pulmonary veins drain to the right atrium via
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: an intracardiac connection, generally the coronary sinus, or directly to the right atrium. Mixed type—Anomalous pulmonary venous connections
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: occur at two or more levels. Typically, the left pulmonary veins may drain into the systemic veins through an ascending vertical vein (supracardiac), and the right pulmonary veins drain into the coronary sinus or directly into the right atrium (cardiac). Other complex variants have been reported as well (Fig. 76.4).
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The supracardiac form is most common, occurring in roughly half of cases, and the mixed form is the least common. Infracardiac TAPVC in particular may present in extremis in the neonatal period due to obstruction of the descending vertical vein at the diaphragm, the ductus venosus, or the portal vein. The supracardiac form less commonly presents with obstruction when the vertical vein passes between the left bronchus and the left pulmonary artery or at the junction of the SVC and the innominate vein. In TAPVC, oxygenated pulmonary venous return mixes completely with deoxygenated systemic venous flow in the right atrium. Systemic blood flow is dependent on the obligatory shunting from the right atrium to the left atrium through an atrial level defect. In the absence of pulmonary venous obstruction, pulmonary blood flow is increased and hypoxia is mild. In contrast, if the anomalous pulmonary venous connection is obstructed
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: along its course, it results in pulmonary venous hypertension with pulmonary edema and decreased pulmonary blood flow. The combination of decreased pulmonary blood flow and impaired pulmonary function caused by edema produces profound systemic hypoxemia.31
paragraphs.heading: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: An atrial level defect is essential for postnatal survival with TAPVC. Left-sided heart defects, transposition of the great arteries, and TOF have also been reported in association with TAPVC. Neonates with heterotaxy syndrome commonly have associated TAPVC.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: In the neonatal period, unobstructed TAPVC is generally asymptomatic. The diagnosis may be made at an older age secondary to recurrent pneumonia or it is identified by echocardiography during evaluation for a murmur. Cyanosis and respiratory distress are generally seen in infants with the severe forms of obstructed pulmonary venous connections or restrictive atrial communications. In infants without obstruction, volume overload, increased pulmonary blood flow, and inadequate weight gain gradually develop.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Chest radiography is very helpful in TAPVC, as pulmonary edema is highly suggestive of pulmonary venous obstruction. Dilated mediastinal veins give an appearance of fullness to the superior mediastinum (snowman sign), although in neonates this is usually masked by the thymus. ECG findings are nonspecific. Echocardiography is the gold
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: standard, and careful examination of each pulmonary vein entry into the pulmonary venous confluence and drainage site of the confluence is paramount. Signs on prenatal echocardiography such as ventricular disproportion, increased area behind the left atrium, and visualization of a vertical vein can be useful in identifying fetuses with TAPVC.32 Sites of venous obstruction can also be identified via spectral and color flow Doppler imaging. The individual pulmonary vein and confluence sizes should be evaluated, as pulmonary vein diameters less than 2 mm have been associated with a poor prognosis. The atrial level defect must also be evaluated for signs of restriction, and balloon atrial septostomy is recommended when restrictive. Echocardiography is usually diagnostic; however, advanced imaging with cardiac MRI, cardiac CTA (see Fig. 76.4), or cardiac catheterization should be considered in more complex cases.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Unobstructed TAPVC generally requires minimal medical management until the infant is ready for surgical intervention. Neonates with restrictive atrial level defects should undergo balloon atrial septostomy. Neonates with pulmonary venous obstruction tend to be profoundly hypoxic and require significant respiratory and metabolic support; extracorporeal membrane oxygenation has been used as a bridge to complete surgical repair. Urgent neonatal surgery is essential for those with pulmonary venous obstruction. Elective repair via anastomosis of the common pulmonary venous confluence to the left atrium is done in neonates with unobstructed TAPVC in the first months of life. Postoperative pulmonary artery hypertension and pulmonary vascular reactivity are
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: most troublesome in neonates with preoperative pulmonary venous obstruction. The long-term prognosis is excellent except in small neonates with hypoplastic pulmonary veins or single ventricle variants.31 Recurrent or persistent pulmonary venous obstruction at the anastomotic site or the individual pulmonary veins is difficult to treat by either surgery or interventional catheterization, and a sutureless technique for surgical repair has been developed that has shown a lower incidence of these complications.33
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In truncus arteriosus, the brachiocephalic, pulmonary, and coronary arteries arise from a single arterial trunk. This single trunk overrides a large VSD that allows mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous return. In type I, a short main pulmonary artery segment arises from the truncus arteriosus, and it gives rise to the branch pulmonary arteries. In type II, both branch pulmonary arteries have a direct origin from the common trunk. In type III, the pulmonary arteries arise from opposite sides of the common truncus and are remote from each other. Truncus arteriosus with the absence of one pulmonary artery branch and the presence of major AP artery collateral arteries are rare forms.34 Both pulmonary and systemic blood flows are determined by the relative SVRs and PVRs. As the PVR falls, there tends to be increased pulmonary blood flow, resulting in pulmonary overcirculation and increased left atrial and ventricular size.
paragraphs.heading: Truncus Arteriosus Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: A number of other cardiac defects are seen in association with truncus arteriosus. Importantly, the single semilunar truncal valve is often thickened and dysplastic and demonstrates variable morphology, with anywhere from one to six leaflets and differing degrees of valvar stenosis and regurgitation. Unilateral or bilateral branch pulmonary artery stenosis occurs in about 10% of cases. Coronary artery anomalies and stenosis are rare but are surgically important variations.35 A right aortic arch is found in 15% to 25% of patients with truncus arteriosus, and aortic coarctation or interrupted aortic arch may also be present. In addition, 22q11 chromosomal microdeletion (DiGeorge) syndrome is a very common association, and genetic testing should be obtained.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: The neonatal presentation of uncomplicated truncus arteriosus can be subtle, with mild tachypnea and/or cyanosis as the only symptom. Systemic oxygen saturation is generally in the mid-80% range, and it increases as PVR drops and pulmonary blood flow increases. Lower saturation may indicate increased PVR, branch pulmonary artery stenosis, or pulmonary edema. Acidosis can be present in infants with associated truncal stenosis and regurgitation or aortic arch obstruction. As the PVR drops, pulmonary blood flow increases, resulting in signs and symptoms of pulmonary overcirculation. Truncal valve stenosis and regurgitation murmurs can be identified on exam. Infants may have bounding peripheral
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: pulses and increased pulse pressures secondary to decreased diastolic pressure caused by blood flow runoff into the branch pulmonary arteries. Poor perfusion and decreased leg pulses may indicate aortic coarctation or arch interruption. Given the association with 22q11 chromosomal microdeletion syndrome and absent thymus, serum calcium should be monitored in all patients with truncus arteriosus.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Chest radiography in truncus arteriosus typically demonstrates cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vasculature markings. An ECG may show biventricular hypertrophy or be normal. Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosis—attention must be paid to define the truncal valve anatomy and function, branch pulmonary arteries, aortic arch anatomy, and coronary arteries. Cardiac catheterization, CTA, and MRI are reserved for cases where the anatomy has not been well defined by echocardiography. Chromosomal microarray testing should be obtained in all infants with truncus arteriosus.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: In infants with truncus arteriosus, symptoms related to increased pulmonary blood flow generally respond well to diuretics and digoxin. Supplemental oxygen should be avoided, as it decreases PVR, increasing pulmonary blood flow. Infants with moderate to severe truncal valve stenosis or regurgitation generally do not respond well to medical management and may require transcatheter balloon valvuloplasty or early surgical intervention. In 22q11 infants, careful management of calcium levels is required. Truncus arteriosus is typically repaired in the first months of life, and it consists of patch closure of VSD and placement of a right ventricle to pulmonary artery (RV-PA) conduit. Associated defects, including truncal valve stenosis, aortic arch interruption, coronary abnormalities, and branch pulmonary artery atresia, may increase procedural risk but do not preclude it.36 If truncal valve stenosis or regurgitation is severe, surgical replacement may be indicated to provide a competent neoaortic valve. The long-term prognosis for infants with uncomplicated repaired truncus arteriosus is excellent. RV-PA conduit replacement is generally needed by age 5 years in about 20% of patients, and a lifetime of multiple surgical and transcatheter replacements is required. The truncal/neoaortic valve may develop worsening stenosis and can require valve repair or replacement in 25% of patients. Interventions on the RV outflow and pulmonary arteries are performed in over half of these patients at 20 years following their initial operation.37 Ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmias are generally poor prognostic indicators.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Congenital heart disease resulting in single ventricle anatomy or physiology encompasses a wide range of defects
paragraphs.heading: Single Ventricle Anatomy/Physiology

paragraphs.text: and structural variants. A systematic segmental approach to determine a patient’s venous, atrial, ventricular, and arterial connections generally allows accurate diagnosis. Furthermore, basic physiologic principles help guide management in this population. For example, there must be adequate mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous return to support single ventricular output. This mixing occurs most effectively through an atrial level defect (PFO or ASD). Additional shunting and mixing can also occur via a VSD or PDA. The single ventricle predominantly pumps blood to either the systemic or pulmonary circulation, and the predominant circulation must then support the other via shunting through a PDA. Systemic oxygen saturations are determined by the relative resistances across the pulmonary and systemic vascular beds. It is important to recognize that many infants have low PVR, resulting in unrestrictive pulmonary blood flow. Oxygen acts as a pulmonary vasodilator, further increasing pulmonary blood flow, often at the cost of systemic blood flow, and therefore should be used judiciously.
paragraphs.heading: Single Ventricle Anatomy/Physiology

paragraphs.text: When single ventricle anatomy/physiology has been diagnosed, the next step is to determine whether the pulmonary or systemic circulation requires support. This primarily guides the interventions needed for effective management, including long-term surgical planning. Advances in fetal echocardiography have allowed for increased prenatal diagnosis, better expectant management, and collaborative work among obstetrics, pediatric cardiology, intensive care, and cardiothoracic surgery teams to optimize care for these patients and better prepare the affected families for the challenges ahead.
paragraphs.heading: Single Ventricle Anatomy/Physiology

paragraphs.text: Before 1980, no effective palliation was available for infants with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). Staged surgical palliation, including the Norwood operation with its modifications,38 and neonatal cardiac transplantation have offered new hope to the families of newborn infants with this otherwise uniformly lethal cardiac defect. Advances in both approaches have greatly improved the duration and quality of life for these patients.
paragraphs.heading: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

paragraphs.text: HLHS consists of a spectrum of congenital abnormalities of the mitral and aortic valves, ranging from mitral stenosis and aortic stenosis to mitral atresia and aortic atresia in the most severe variants. It then results in variable degrees of LV hypoplasia and ascending aorta and aortic arch hypoplasia. Aortic coarctation may be present, and LV endocardial fibroelastosis can result from in utero subendocardial ischemia. Coronary artery abnormalities have also been identified but have uncertain impact on long-term myocardial function. In HLHS, the systemic circulation is ductal dependent— ductal flow courses retrograde to the transverse arch and ascending aorta to supply the brachiocephalic vessels and coronary arteries, as well as antegrade to the descending
paragraphs.heading: Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: aorta. In utero, when PVR is high, this circulation provides excellent organ perfusion, and fetal growth is usually normal. Postnatally, even as PVR falls and pulmonary blood flow increases, RV output remains adequate to supply both the systemic and pulmonary circulations. However, ductal closure dramatically alters this balance, leading to profound systemic and myocardial hypoperfusion with metabolic acidosis and multisystem organ failure.
paragraphs.heading: Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The most important associated intracardiac defect in HLHS is an unrestrictive atrial level shunt. An absent or restrictive atrial defect in utero creates severe pulmonary venous hypertension, leading to detrimental pulmonary vasculature changes. Significant atrial restriction can result in greatly increased morbidity and mortality in the neonatal period and is a major negative prognostic factor in postnatal outcomes, particularly in the subgroup with mitral or aortic atresia. Fetal diagnosis also allows for consideration of fetal atrial septoplasty or atrial stent implantation in the select patient with a restrictive atrial septum.39,62 Other important associated defects for HLHS include pulmonary venous return anomalies. Occasional neonates with aortic atresia may have a normal-sized mitral valve and left ventricle because of an associated VSD. Central nervous system anomalies, including absent corpus callosum, are also quite common in infants with HLHS. Furthermore, there is increasing recognition of the in utero effects of congenital heart disease, including HLHS, on prenatal brain development and postnatal neurodevelopmental outcomes.40
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: Increasing prenatal diagnosis of HLHS has greatly helped prepare families and improve coordination between the medical teams involved in the delivery and initial management of these infants. Infants with HLHS often have tachypnea and mild cyanosis in the postnatal period. There can be a moderately increased RV impulse on exam, a single second heart sound, and variable murmurs. With ductal patency, pulses can be nearly normal. Pulse oximetry varies widely, ranging from 70% to greater than 90%, depending on the amount of pulmonary blood flow and degree of pulmonary edema. A restrictive atrial level defect can produce significant pulmonary edema because of increased left atrial pressure and resultant increased pulmonary venous pressure. The combination of pulmonary edema and restricted pulmonary blood flow produces profound hypoxia.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The ECG in HLHS generally demonstrates dominant RV forces, often with a QR pattern in the right chest leads. Chest radiography shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary blood flow with more prominent pulmonary vascular markings and pulmonary venous congestion. Echocardiography (Fig. 76.5) defines the underlying anatomy, including the atrial level defect and its degree of restriction, atrioventricular valve regurgitation, ventricular function, outflow tract
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: obstruction, coronary anatomy, and aortic arch morphology, as well as possible associated systemic or pulmonary venous return anomalies. Delineating the anatomy is essential prior to any type of intervention.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: In HLHS, the systemic circulation is ductal dependent, and maintaining ductal patency in the immediate postnatal period with intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion is critical for survival. In patients with a severely restrictive ASD, balloon atrial septostomy can be performed to reduce pulmonary venous pressure and pulmonary edema.41 Beyond this period, a staged surgical approach is used in most centers. Neonatal cardiac transplantation42 remains an option but is greatly limited by donor heart availability. A hybrid approach combined with ventricular assist device insertion can be used as a bridge to transplantation in suboptimal candidates for Norwood palliation.43 No matter the chosen strategy, careful postnatal assessment and management to prevent complications from excessive pulmonary blood flow are essential for good long-term results. The overall goal of staged surgical palliation for HLHS is to separate the systemic and pulmonary circulations in a stepwise fashion while ensuring adequate systemic blood flow at each stage and protecting the pulmonary vasculature from excessive flow and pulmonary hypertension. Surgical and interventional techniques in addition to postsurgical management have evolved greatly over a number of decades to address the various issues that have been recognized during the evolution of the current staged approach.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In most centers, initial (stage I) surgical palliation is done in the immediate postnatal period with a Norwood
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: procedure, including aortic reconstruction, systemic-topulmonary arterial shunt placement (modified Blalock- Thomas-Taussig [mBTT] shunt or RV-PA conduit [Sano modification]), and atrial septectomy. A Damus-Kaye- Stansel anastomosis may be utilized if the ascending aorta is of sufficient size.44 Stage I palliation may also be accomplished via a hybrid procedure done by surgical and interventional catheterization teams working in tandem. Hybrid stage I palliation consists of surgical bilateral branch pulmonary artery banding and transcatheter PDA stent placement. The theoretical advantages of this approach are avoidance of cardiopulmonary bypass and circulatory arrest (and their potential associated adverse effects) in the neonatal period and delay of major aortic intervention/reconstruction to an older age when infants are larger. This approach can be complicated by the need for ongoing catheter interventions on branch pulmonary arteries following subsequent staged surgeries.45 The primary goals of both Norwood and hybrid stage I palliation are to provide adequate systemic blood flow and to effectively control pulmonary blood flow. Postoperative management requires very close monitoring of systemic perfusion and appropriate cardiovascular and respiratory support as needed to avoid tissue/organ hypoxia. Typical systemic arterial saturations following stage I palliation are in the mid-70% to mid-80% range. Even with greatly improved surgical and intensive care techniques, a proportion of infants after stage I palliation require extracorporeal membrane oxygenation support to achieve stability with eventual poor results.46,62
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Following either stage I technique, stage II palliation entails completing a superior cavopulmonary (Glenn shunt) anastomosis or hemi-Fontan procedure to allow the SVC flow to directly drain into the pulmonary arteries.47 In the hybrid approach, the previously deferred aortic reconstruction must also be completed, and the total operation is denoted a comprehensive stage II procedure. Stage II palliation is typically completed between 4 and 6 months of age and results in systemic venous return from the upper body (via the SVC) as the sole source of pulmonary blood flow. Because SVC flow no longer drains to the systemic single ventricle, the ventricular volume loading is reduced, lessening its overall workload and reducing the potential for ventricular dysfunction. Typical systemic arterial saturations following stage II palliation climb into the mid-70% to mid-80% range.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Staged surgical palliation for HLHS is completed at approximately 2 to 4 years of age via a total cavopulmonary connection (Fontan procedure) to direct inferior vena cava drainage to the pulmonary arteries. A number of different surgical techniques have been utilized through the years and are now grouped together as Fontan variants, including direct atriopulmonary anastomosis (the classic Fontan first done in 1973 is no longer utilized), intracardiac connection (lateral tunnel Fontan), and extracardiac conduit connection (extracardiac Fontan), with or without fenestration in the Fontan conduit.48,62 Following any
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Fontan variant, the pulmonary and systemic circulations are separated, with the single systemic ventricle receiving oxygenated pulmonary venous return and supplying the systemic circulation in a pulsatile fashion and systemic venous return passively draining to the lungs via the cavopulmonary anastomoses. This generally results in systemic arterial saturations greater than 90% but typically not normal due to continued mixing of coronary venous drainage into the systemic ventricle and sometimes due to the presence of venous collaterals.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: The evolution of the current staged surgical palliation strategy for HLHS has been an iterative process with great advances achieved due to the coordinated and dedicated efforts of entire medical teams and heart centers, including nursing, social work, and multiple medical and surgical specialties. Mortality and morbidity were high during the development of the Norwood procedure, and early experiences with stage I palliation resulted in 1-year survival rates less than 50%. These results have greatly improved into the current era, and staged single ventricle palliation has resulted in significantly increased survival and quality of life.49 A multicenter prospective clinical trial comparing the mBTT shunt and Sano modification in Norwood stage I palliation failed to show any major differences between the two procedures. Most series comparing the different stage I strategies, including the hybrid approach, have failed to demonstrate a significant difference in outcomes, but some data do demonstrate a survival benefit with the Norwood-Sano technique in certain HLHS variants, with recent studies suggesting more favorable neurodevelopment following an initial hybrid approach.50 Risk factors for poor stage I survival include low birth weight, a restrictive atrial level defect, ventricular dysfunction, and significant atrioventricular (AV) valve regurgitation. Interstage mortality (between stage I and stage II palliation) remains a complicated, vexing issue. Long-term morbidity and mortality may occur secondary to recurrent coarctation or arch obstruction, AV valve regurgitation, sinus node dysfunction, various arrhythmias, and ventricular dysfunction. Fontan-associated liver disease has received increased attention as long-term survival continues to increase in the single ventricle population.51 Increasing data also demonstrate the association between HLHS and higher risk for neurodevelopmental issues.40
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In double outlet right ventricle (DORV), the aorta and the pulmonary artery both arise from the right ventricle. There are four distinct subtypes based on the location of the VSD and its relationship to the great arteries: (1) subaortic, (2) subpulmonary, (3) doubly committed, or (4) remote from the great arteries. The Taussig-Bing malformation is a DORV variant with a subpulmonary VSD and D-malposition of the aorta, typically side-by-side with the pulmonary artery. DORV physiology is determined
paragraphs.heading: Double Outlet Right Ventricle Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: by VSD location and associated defects, ranging from excessive pulmonary blood flow from a large VSD shunt physiology to transposition physiology due to streaming of blood flow.
paragraphs.heading: Double Outlet Right Ventricle Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Commonly associated defects in DORV are subvalvar and/ or valvar PS. In DORV with a subaortic VSD and PS, the physiology is similar to TOF. In the Taussig-Bing variant where the blood flow is preferentially directed toward the pulmonary artery, associated aortic arch anomalies, including coarctation or interruption, are often seen.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: The clinical presentation of DORV in the neonatal period can vary widely and include significant cyanosis in transposition variants or when there is associated severe PS or atresia, or shock and cardiovascular collapse with ductal closure in Taussig-Bing variants with coarctation of the aorta or interrupted aortic arch. As the PVR drops, tachypnea may develop if pulmonary blood flow is unrestricted. A murmur generally suggests the presence of PS, which may protect the pulmonary vascular bed and result in a well-balanced circulation with mild cyanosis.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The ECG and chest radiograph in DORV are nonspecific. Echocardiography is used to delineate its features, including VSD location, size, and relationship to the great arteries. The great artery configuration and relationship to each other, the presence of PS, and aortic arch abnormalities should be easily identified.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Surgical intervention for DORV is dependent on the predominant physiology, as well as VSD location and its relationship to the great arteries and associated lesions. Hence, definitive repair could simply entail VSD closure or become increasingly complex to involve components such as an arterial switch operation or coarctation/interrupted arch repair, or the need for initial systemic-to-pulmonary artery shunt followed by right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery conduit later in infancy.52 DORV repair is generally performed in the first 6 months of life.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Isolated aortic valve disease ranges from asymptomatic bicuspid aortic valves to critical valvar aortic stenosis. Mild to moderate aortic valve stenosis is well tolerated in utero, generally resulting in LV hypertrophy. Severe aortic stenosis in utero leads to significant LV hypertrophy and compromised coronary circulation, sometimes resulting in endocardial fibroelastosis and eventual LV dilation and
paragraphs.heading: Valvar Aortic Stenosis Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: systolic and diastolic dysfunction. Ductal patency is often required to maintain adequate systemic output.
paragraphs.heading: Valvar Aortic Stenosis Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: Mild aortic stenosis can be accompanied by a large PDA, which may exaggerate the pressure gradient across the aortic valve due to increased pulmonary venous return to the left heart. Associated significant aortic insufficiency is uncommon in neonatal aortic stenosis. If present, it should raise suspicion for a tunnel from the LV to the aorta. Aortic root dilation of variable degree can be seen in neonatal aortic stenosis. Supravalvar aortic stenosis should prompt evaluation for Williams syndrome.53 Diffuse aortic root and/or ascending aorta hypoplasia can be a sign of associated aortic coarctation or left heart hypoplasia with severe aortic valve stenosis.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: The cardinal physical finding in neonatal aortic stenosis is a systolic ejection murmur radiating upward to the neck. Its intensity and length are dependent on the severity of stenosis, ventricular function, and cardiac output. A systolic ejection click may also be appreciated at the apex of the heart. In critical aortic stenosis, ductal patency is required for adequate systemic perfusion, as ductal closure can lead to rapid cardiovascular collapse, shock, metabolic acidosis, and multiorgan failure.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Because the severity of neonatal aortic stenosis may be difficult to fully assess clinically, thorough diagnostic assessment is essential. The ECG is usually normal or may show LV hypertrophy. Chest radiography may show pulmonary edema. Echocardiography (Fig. 76.6) is the standard imaging modality to define the aortic valve anatomy, degree of stenosis by spectral Doppler (see Fig. 76.6B), presence of ventricular dysfunction, and associated defects, including
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: mitral valve abnormalities, aortic enlargement, PDA, and coarctation the aorta. Pulse oximetry differential between the upper and lower extremities suggests right-to-left shunting at the ductal level due to pulmonary hypertension. Arterial blood gas and serum biomarkers can be followed to assess tissue perfusion.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Mild valvar aortic stenosis is well tolerated, with no immediate intervention required aside from outpatient follow-up. Moderate to severe aortic stenosis can progress in the first few months of life, necessitating closer follow-up. Evidence of inadequate systemic perfusion or ventricular dysfunction in an infant with severe aortic stenosis is an indication for balloon or surgical valvotomy.54 Critical aortic stenosis is a neonatal emergency and continues to result in relatively high morbidity and mortality when not expediently diagnosed and intervened upon. Success rates with neonatal balloon aortic valvuloplasty have been good and considered acceptable when faced with the alternative of surgery, but the procedure can result in residual stenosis or variable degrees of iatrogenic insufficiency, eventually necessitating reintervention.55 Surgical valvotomy remains an alternative as a primary intervention or secondary measure if balloon aortic valvuloplasty is unsuccessful. If the aortic valve or LV is deemed unsuitable for these procedures, single ventricle palliation might be a more suitable long-term solution.49,56 In the case of infants presenting with a borderline left ventricle, determining the suitability for a two-ventricle approach can be challenging, and staged palliation has been proposed.57
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Aortic development is a complex embryologic process that can lead to a number of aortic arch variants and pathologic anomalies. The most common obstructive aortic arch
paragraphs.heading: Aortic Coarctation and Interrupted Aortic Arch Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: abnormality is aortic coarctation. In its most simple form, it consists of a discrete narrowing in the juxtaductal region of the distal arch/aortic isthmus where the PDA joins the aorta. In more severe forms, there may be associated transverse aortic arch and isthmic hypoplasia. The most severe form of aortic arch obstruction is an interrupted aortic arch (IAA) with complete aortic discontinuity. IAA is classified according to the location of the discontinuity in relation to the head and neck vessel origins. In type A IAA, the interruption occurs distal to the last head and neck vessel (typically the left subclavian artery) in the distal arch/isthmic region. In type B IAA, the interruption occurs more proximally between the second and third head and neck vessels (typically the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries). In type C IAA, the interruption occurs further proximally between the first and second head and neck vessels (typically the innominate and left common carotid arteries). IAA type B is the most common IAA variant, occurring in just over half of cases. In both aortic coarctation and IAA, abnormalities of the head and neck vessel origins (e.g., aberrant subclavian artery) may be present. IAA and hemodynamically significant aortic coarctation result in systemic hypertension, increased LV afterload, and LV hypertrophy. Severe aortic obstruction from a severe coarctation or IAA can lead to LV failure and inadequate perfusion distal to the obstruction, particularly with ductal closure. Thus maintenance of ductal patency is critical to survival and well-being in these infants prior to intervention. Conversely, a significant coarctation may be unmasked during ductal closure. Aside from effects on the LV myocardium, neonatal coarctation may also affect the RV myocardium due to LV diastolic dysfunction, pulmonary venous congestion, pulmonary hypertension, and interventricular interactions, leading to RV hypertrophy and dysfunction.
paragraphs.heading: Aortic Coarctation and Interrupted Aortic Arch Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The most common defects associated with aortic coarctation are bicuspid aortic valve (50% to almost 85% of cases in some series) and VSD. Mitral valve anomalies may also be present. IAA is commonly associated with posterior malalignment VSD resulting in subaortic stenosis. Other associated lesions include AP window, truncus arteriosus, and transposition of the great arteries. Both aortic coarctation and IAA may complicate other forms of complex congenital heart disease. With regard to genetic disorders, aortic coarctation has a known association with Turner syndrome, and IAA can be seen with partial or complete 22q11 chromosomal microdeletion syndrome, particularly in the setting of a right aortic arch.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: Mild aortic coarctation with no associated valvar aortic stenosis or VSD is generally asymptomatic. Infants will often have diminished femoral pulses on exam but no other outward signs or symptoms. More severe cases can lead to tachypnea, tachycardia, poor feeding, and lethargy, particularly as the ductus arteriosus spontaneously closes. In critical
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: coarctation or IAA, rapid cardiovascular collapse with shock, hypoperfusion, and multiorgan dysfunction can occur with ductal closure. The hallmarks of significant arch obstruction are diminished femoral pulses and blood pressure and oxygen saturation differentials between the upper and lower extremities, although all these may be less pronounced in the setting of dysfunction. Careful assessment of all peripheral pulses can be valuable. Blood pressure should be measured on all four extremities to evaluate for discrepancies. Tachycardia, precordial hyperactivity, single second heart sound, a gallop rhythm, and hepatomegaly are markers of significant obstruction and possible associated defects. The typical systolic murmur of aortic coarctation—most prominent over the left infraclavicular region and under the left scapula—is well appreciated in older children with coarctation but may not be heard in neonates.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The ECG of a neonate with aortic coarctation or IAA may demonstrate LV hypertrophy. Chest radiographs are usually normal. Significant cardiomegaly suggests associated lesions or ventricular dilation or dysfunction following ductal closure. Echocardiography is used to define the arch obstruction, aortic arch and branching anatomy, and associated lesions. Ascertaining coarctation severity in the presence of a sizable PDA can be difficult, as the aortic isthmus may be surrounded by ductal tissue. Echocardiography is usually sufficient to diagnose most aortic arch abnormalities; however, advanced imaging with cardiac MRI or cardiac computed tomography can be helpful in more complex cases. Fig. 76.8 shows a shows a three-dimensional, volumerendered reconstruction of a CT angiogram in a neonate with coarctation. Clinically significant neonatal coarctation can also produce moderate to severe right heart dysfunction. Right-to-left shunting at the ductal level is an important sign of significant obstruction and pulmonary hypertension. Transverse arch hypoplasia, especially with an elongated segment between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries, also suggests significant aortic coarctation. Pre- and postductal pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas measurements in the upper and lower extremities are instrumental in assessing ductal shunting and perfusion.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Neonates with aortic coarctation or IAA presenting with signs or symptoms of congestive heart failure or low cardiac output must be started on intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain or restore ductal patency. All neonates with IAA undergo early surgical repair of the aortic arch abnormality and associated defects. Long-term results with IAA and AP window or VSD are good, but recurrent arch obstruction and subaortic stenosis are frequent problems.58 Mortality and morbidity in newborns with IAA and truncus arteriosus remain significant. Those with significant arch hypoplasia might require mobilization of the descending aorta to provide enough tissue to relieve the obstruction. Neonates with aortic coarctation and a large VSD undergo
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: early complete repair.59 Simple (noncritical) aortic coarctation, on the other hand, is repaired electively in early childhood. Indications for early repair in infancy include systemic hypertension, ventricular dysfunction, or cardiovascular collapse with ductal closure. Surgical repair remains the gold standard for primary intervention. A number of surgical techniques have been used, but in the absence of hemodynamically significant intracardiac defects, coarctation resection and end-to-end anastomosis repair through a lateral thoracotomy approach is utilized.60 Extended end-to-end anastomosis repair with arch augmentation through a medial sternotomy may be needed when there is associated transverse aortic arch hypoplasia. Balloon angioplasty of native aortic coarctation is usually reserved for older children but might be useful in the treatment of selected neonates, particularly as a palliative procedure, and it remains a topic of considerable debate. Postoperative systemic hypertension, a very common occurrence following coarctation repair in older children, occurs less frequently in neonates. However, long-term growth of the repaired aortic segment might be an issue in up to 30% of infants, resulting in significant aortic narrowing or recurrent coarctation, particularly in premature infants. Balloon aortic angioplasty has become the preferred treatment for recurrent coarctation in infants and young children, with demonstrated safety and efficacy.61
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: When any level of left heart obstruction is suspected, the entire left heart must be thoroughly evaluated with echocardiography, as additional left-sided obstructive lesions may be present. Mitral valve abnormalities are commonly encountered, and these can involve the leaflets, chordae as in mitral valve arcade, or papillary muscles anomalies, including single mitral valve papillary muscle resulting in a parachute deformity.62 Supravalvar mitral rings and subaortic membranes can also be present and may become progressively obstructive, necessitating close longitudinal follow-up and eventually surgical repair. Shone complex consists of three or more left heart obstructive lesions, which can include supravalvar mitral ring, parachute or arcade mitral valve, subaortic stenosis, and aortic coarctation, resulting in multilevel obstruction.63
paragraphs.heading: Serial Obstructive Left Heart Defects

paragraphs.text: Isolated neonatal valvar pulmonary stenosis (PS) most commonly results from dysplasia of the valve leaflets with resultant thickening and decreased mobility, leading to varying degrees of obstruction at the valvar level. Associated RV hypertension and hypertrophy occur in proportion to obstruction severity. Post-stenotic main pulmonary artery dilation is also commonly found. The direction of atrial and ventricular level shunts, when present, is usually determined by the degree of RV hypertension and RV compliance.
paragraphs.heading: Valvar Pulmonary Stenosis Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The most commonly associated abnormality with PS is fixed or dynamic subvalvar (infundibular) narrowing or stenosis. The combined subvalvar/valvar RVOT obstruction can be overestimated when atrial or ventricular shunts are present or underestimated in the setting of increased PVR (especially in the immediate postnatal period) or RV dysfunction. Valvar PS may also be seen in association with genetic disorders such as Noonan syndrome.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: Neonates with PS generally remain asymptomatic in the postnatal period and are initially identified via auscultation of a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the infraclavicular areas and over the back. Murmur intensity correlates with obstruction severity. In moderate to severe PS, an increased RV impulse may be noted.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Pulmonary valve morphology and extent of the pulmonary outflow obstruction are delineated by echocardiography. The RVOT and pulmonary valve gradients are measured by spectral Doppler. Neonates with mild valvar PS may not be initially diagnosed until they are noted to have a murmur beyond the immediate postnatal period as PVR falls and the
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: pressure gradient across the RVOT and murmur intensity increase.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: The natural history of isolated valvar PS is excellent. In mild cases, most studies demonstrate minimal progression and spontaneous resolution in the majority of cases. However, up to a third of patients in some series may progress to moderate or severe levels of obstruction, typically in the first 6 months to 1 year of life. In rare cases of critical PS with ductal-dependent pulmonary blood flow, neonatal transcatheter balloon valvuloplasty or surgical valvotomy may be necessary. Generally, neonatal valvar PS should be longitudinally followed over the first 6 to 12 months of life to monitor for progression of the obstruction. Transcatheter pulmonary balloon valvuloplasty is indicated for severe PS, and the timing is determined by the RVOT/ pulmonary valve gradient, degree of RV hypertrophy, or presence of RV dysfunction by echocardiography. Even in severe cases, infants with isolated valvar PS are rarely symptomatic. In the current era, surgical pulmonary valvotomy is reserved for patients with significantly dysplastic valves not responsive to balloon valvuloplasty or valvar PS with concomitant intracardiac defects requiring surgical repair.64
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Ventricular septation is a complex embryologic process involving the development and fusion of the muscular ventricular septum, membranous area, conal or outlet septum, and atrioventricular endocardial cushions to form the interventricular septum. Abnormalities in this process result in VSDs, which are the most common forms of congenital heart defects, making up 20% of identified lesions in some population studies. They are classified according to their anatomic location: perimembranous, muscular, inlet, or malalignment or conal septal defects. Perimembranous VSDs are the most common, representing approximately 80% of cases. The amount of shunting through these defects is determined by their size, number, and relative PVRs and SVRs. In the immediate neonatal period, when PVR and RV pressures are high, left-to-right flow may be limited. However, with normal postnatal physiologic transition, PVR falls significantly over the first hours to days of life, with continued gradual decrease toward adult levels within the first 6 to 8 weeks. This results in lower RV pressures and increased left-to-right shunting. With sizable defects, signs and symptoms of pulmonary overcirculation develop, leading to left atrial and LV enlargement.
paragraphs.heading: Ventricular Septal Defect Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: VSDs are often present in more complex forms of congenital heart disease, including many of the lesions discussed in
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: this chapter. Their location, size, and number can affect the presentation and clinical course of other associated lesions such as D-TGA, DORV, and coarctation of the aorta.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: VSDs can be identified by a characteristic holosystolic murmur usually best heard at the left lower sternal border, generated by the left-to-right shunt through the defect. The pitch and duration of the murmur are determined by the size, location of the VSD, and pressure differences between the LV and RV. The common small, pressure-restrictive perimembranous VSD will produce a harsh holosystolic murmur and a possible palpable thrill. A murmur from a small muscular defect may be softer and short as the left-to-right shunt ceases during ventricular systole when surrounded by muscle. Larger VSDs can be more difficult to identify in the immediate postnatal period, given the elevated PVR and less disturbed shunt flow in the setting of nearly equal LV and RV pressures. Similarly, clinical evidence of significant left-toright shunting and resultant pulmonary overcirculation may not become apparent until the PVR drops after the immediate neonatal period. Many newborns with isolated VSDs are discharged home with no symptoms and may not be diagnosed until the initial outpatient followup visits.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Smaller VSDs are routinely diagnosed with careful clinical examination, given their characteristic murmur location and quality. Anatomic type, size, number, direction of blood flow, mechanisms of closure such as surrounding tricuspid valve tissue, or aortic valve prolapse and associated defects are well defined by echocardiography.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Most VSDs require no intervention and undergo spontaneous closure within the first few months to years of life, particularly small to medium perimembranous and muscular defects. These are usually hemodynamically insignificant, and patients remain asymptomatic. Larger VSDs of any type can result in considerable left-to-right shunting, signs and symptoms of pulmonary overcirculation including tachypnea, increased work of breathing, diaphoresis with feedings, feeding difficulties, and suboptimal weight gain. These symptoms in association with LV enlargement are indications for initiation of oral diuretics to help reduce pulmonary symptoms and to improve feedings and growth. Exposure to long-term significant left-to-right shunting can lead to maladaptive pulmonary vascular changes and increased risks for development of pulmonary vaso-occlusive disease. Indications for surgical VSD closure include persistent respiratory symptoms, frequent respiratory infections despite anticongestive therapy, inadequate growth despite optimized nutrition and medical therapy, evidence of pulmonary hypertension, aortic valve leaflet prolapse, development and progression
