paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: of aortic valve insufficiency, or defect types not expected to spontaneously close such as conal septal, subarterial, or malalignment defects.
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: Similar to ventricular septation, embryologic atrial septation is complex, and derangements in the process can result in abnormal interatrial communications. ASDs are classified according to their location and embryologic origin. The major types of ASDs are ostium secundum, ostium primum, and sinus venosus (SVC and IVC types); also, although coronary sinus defects are not truly ASDs, they result in left-to-right shunts and are often included in the classification. Secundum ASDs are the most common, representing over two-thirds of cases. Primum ASDs are a component of atrioventricular septal defects, and sinus venosus ASDs can be associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return. Isolated secundum ASDs diagnosed during the neonatal period are generally an incidental finding, and differentiating small defects from stretched foramen ovale can be challenging. True secundum ASDs including large defects rarely cause symptoms in neonates and infants when isolated and in the absence of comorbidities such as prematurity and its related respiratory complications. Isolated small to moderate secundum ASDs often close spontaneously over time. However, more sizable secundum ASDs must be longitudinally monitored, as they lead to right heart enlargement and may have to be closed during the preschool age, usually between 4 and 6 years of age. When amenable, transcatheter ASD device occlusion has become the preferred approach, with excellent results in children.65
paragraphs.heading: Atrial Septal Defect

paragraphs.text: Atrioventricular canal defects (AVCDs) represent a spectrum of abnormalities resulting from failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse during embryologic cardiac development. The most severe form is a complete AVCD, consisting of an ostium primum ASD, inlet VSD, and common AV valve. Other commonly seen variants include partial AVCD (ostium primum ASD with a cleft mitral valve) and transitional AVCD (ostium primum ASD, cleft mitral valve, and small inlet VSD). The pathophysiology of any AVCD variant depends on the size of the defects and resultant shunting. For example, the physiology of a partial or transitional AVCD mirrors that of a simple ASD, as the majority of shunting occurs at the atrial level. The physiology of a complete AVCD, with sizeable atrial and ventricular septal defects on the other hand, combines ASD and VSD physiology and significant volume overload. These lesions are rarely symptomatic in the immediate neonatal period in the absence of other defects or conditions.
paragraphs.heading: Atrioventricular Septal Defect Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The common AV valve in AVCD is often structurally abnormal, and varying degrees of regurgitation are common. Common AV valve abnormalities may also cause unbalanced ventricular development, leading to right- or left-ventricular dominance. In more extreme cases, this produces single ventricle anatomy and physiology. A common atrium with near complete absence of the atrial septum can be found in some variants, and associated systemic and pulmonary venous anomalies may also be present in the more complex forms. Complete AV canal defects can be seen in association with TOF and DORV, and it is seen in 20% to 30% of trisomy 21 patients.66
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: Significant common AV valve regurgitation can be appreciated as a holosystolic murmur at the apex on exam. It can lead to pulmonary venous congestion and pulmonary edema and can present with tachypnea and increased work of breathing. The large ostium primum ASD and inlet VSD components of the complete atrioventricular canal do not tend to produce significant or characteristic murmurs, particularly in the immediate postnatal period when the PVR is elevated, limiting the extra pulmonary blood flow from the large left-to-right shunts. Systemic oxygen saturation tends to be normal, and cyanosis is generally seen in more complex variants, such as the unbalanced forms with single ventricle physiology or associated TOF.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: The ECG in neonates with AVCD can be characteristic with significant left-axis deviation and right atrial enlargement. The axis deviation results from displacement of the conduction pathways away from their usual locations because of the intracardiac defects. The AVCD type, the atrial and ventricular component sizes, ventricular balance, AV valve morphology and function, outflow tracts, and associated lesions are all well defined by echocardiography.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: A balanced, complete AVCD with no significant common AV valve abnormalities, ventricular dysfunction, or outflow tract anomalies is usually electively repaired during the first 4 to 6 months of life with a high degree of success.67 Infants with trisomy 21 sometimes undergo earlier repair because of the potential for early development of significant pulmonary hypertension. Following complete repair, long-term issues primarily involve AV valve function (stenosis or regurgitation) and development of LV outflow tract obstruction due to accessory AV valve tissue or more complex mechanisms. Infants with partial AV canal defects and no significant MV insufficiency can often wait until the preschool years for complete surgical repair. When more significant MV insufficiency, respiratory symptoms, or growth issues are present, surgical repair is recommended at an earlier age.

paragraphs.heading: Patent Ductus Arteriosus

paragraphs.text: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta in utero, and it is essential during fetal life. Given the high fetal PVR, only 10% to 15% of blood ejected by the right ventricle goes to the lungs, and the remaining flows through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta. The ductus arteriosus generally undergoes spontaneous closure in the immediate postnatal period, and the entire RV output is then ejected into the lungs. If the ductus arteriosus remains patent postnatally, the shunt becomes primarily left to right (aorta to pulmonary artery) as PVR falls in normal fashion, resulting in left atrial and LV volume overload. An important exception to this pattern of left heart volume overload occurs in neonates with persistent transitional circulation where the PVR is comparable to or higher than the SVR, resulting in bidirectional shunting through the PDA. If PVR is significantly higher than SVR, the shunting becomes exclusively right to left (pulmonary artery to aorta), causing systemic oxygen desaturations.
paragraphs.heading: Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: The mechanisms responsible for postnatal ductal closure are not fully understood. The ductus arteriosus is highly sensitive to changes in oxygen tension, so the normal postnatal increase in arterial oxygen tension may serve as the stimulus for ductal closure. The mediation of this response is less certain and is likely attributable to a complex interaction among autonomic chemical mediators, prostaglandins, and the ductal musculature. The ductus arteriosus functionally closes in most full-term infants during the first 24 hours of life, but anatomic obliteration of the ductus arteriosus generally does not occur until after the first week of life. A persistent PDA is uncommon in otherwise normal children. In contrast, 30% of infants with birth weight less than 1.5 kg have a PDA, possibly as a result of hypoxia and immaturity of the ductal closure mechanisms, and spontaneous PDA closure by the fourth postnatal day only occurs in approximately one-third of infants weighing less than 1000 g.68 Therefore a majority of very premature infants with hemodynamically significant PDA are potential candidates for pharmacologic, transcatheter, or surgical intervention, although the indications for these interventions remain controversial.
paragraphs.heading: Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: A PDA is present at birth in newborns with all but a few congenital heart defects. Although the presenting features of the associated defects are usually clear, occasionally the PDA is the most easily recognized component clinically and by echocardiography. Aortic coarctation in particular can be difficult to definitively diagnose in the presence of a large PDA. Absence of the ductus arteriosus is notable in some neonates with TOF and pulmonary atresia. In these cases,
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: the central pulmonary arteries are markedly hypoplastic where the ductus arteriosus would insert, and multiple AP collateral vessels may be present. The ductus arteriosus is also often absent in newborns with the absent pulmonary valve TOF variant in which failure of ductal development or closure at a critical time in cardiogenesis may play a role in the pathogenesis of the pulmonary valve and arterial abnormalities.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: The murmur heard in a neonate with a PDA may be unlike that heard in an older infant or child with a persistent PDA, where the classic continuous (machinery) murmur is present. In newborns and infants, especially in the setting of prematurity, diastolic flow through the PDA may be limited due to persistently elevated PVR, and it is consequently difficult to hear. A systolic murmur of uneven intensity throughout systole may be appreciated at the left upper sternal border, peripheral pulses are usually accentuated or bounding, and pulse pressure is increased in a hemodynamically significant PDA. Even in the absence of a murmur, however, significant left-to-right shunting with resultant increased blood flow may result in a supplemental oxygen requirement or cause ventilator weaning difficulties in infants with existing respiratory failure. Clinical evidence of a hemodynamically significant PDA may lag behind echocardiographic findings.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: In symptomatic infants, the presence of a PDA should be confirmed by echocardiography (Fig. 76.8), which can also provide data reflecting the hemodynamic significance of the shunt such as the degree of left heart
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: enlargement, estimation of pulmonary artery pressures, and presence of associated lesions. Chest radiography may demonstrate pulmonary vascular congestion but is generally not diagnostic. Serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), produced in response to myocardial stretch from chamber enlargement, may be a useful bedside screening tool to guide response to therapy in premature infants with PDA.69
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Full-term infants with a small PDA are followed clinically, and spontaneous ductal closure generally occurs in the first months of life. Isolated moderate or large PDAs may also close spontaneously over time but require longitudinal follow-up, with periodic imaging using echocardiography to monitor for interval changes in the left atrial and LV size and to estimate RV pressure as the result of left-to-right shunting. Conventional surgical closure, videoassisted thoracoscopic surgery,70 and transcatheter occlusion are interventional options for newborns and infants with a moderate to large sized PDA. Newer devices such as specifically designed ductal occluders have led to increased experience with transcatheter interventions with excellent results and minimal complications.71
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: In premature infants, spontaneous ductal closure is common, but persistent or recurrent symptoms, respiratory distress, or failure exacerbated by excessive pulmonary blood flow may require therapy for ductal closure. The optimal approach to the PDA in preterm infants is still unknown. A proportion of infants will have spontaneous closure over the first week of life. Thus some have advocated for delaying assessment of patency until the end of the first week of life. However, there is concern that prolonged exposure to a large hemodynamically significant PDA may compromise the pulmonary vascular bed and may be associated with an increased risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.72 Progressive increases in ventilator or supplemental oxygen support requirements may also be manifestations of an increasingly hemodynamically significant PDA. Medical management with fluid restriction and diuretics is occasionally effective at improving symptomatology. Indomethacin, a prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor, and ibuprofen, a nonselective cyclooxygenase inhibitor, have both been shown to effectively close persistent PDAs in a large number of premature newborns up to 14 days of age and occasionally as late as 1 month of age. Ibuprofen has been further shown to have fewer renal side effects. Repeated courses of indomethacin or ibuprofen may be effective in infants who do not respond to the first or second course. Acetaminophen is gaining favor as an equally effective alternative for PDA closure with fewer adverse effects,72a but its role in optimal management of preterm infants with PDA remains to be established. Surgical PDA ligation is also an option but has been associated with increased morbidity and adverse
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: neurodevelopmental outcomes, as well as a relatively high incidence of postoperative left vocal cord paralysis in extremely low birth weight infants.73 Surgical intervention remains a consideration if a PDA remains hemodynamically significant by clinical or echocardiographic criteria following indomethacin or ibuprofen therapies or if pharmacotherapy is contraindicated. There is also increasing evidence for effective transcatheter ductal occlusion in extremely premature and very low birth weight infants weighing less than 1 kg.74
paragraphs.heading: Management and Prognosis

paragraphs.text: An aortopulmonary (AP) window, as its name implies, is an abnormal connection between the ascending aorta and the main pulmonary artery. It results from failure of the conotruncal ridges to fuse during cardiac development. The defects tend to be large, allowing high-pressure shunting from the systemic to the pulmonary circulation, leading to considerable pulmonary overcirculation. AP window pathophysiology mimics that of a large VSD or PDA with significant left-to-right shunting that increases as the PVR falls.
paragraphs.heading: Aortopulmonary Window Anatomy and Pathophysiology

paragraphs.text: AP windows can be present in conjunction with other cardiac anomalies in approximately half of cases, including other conotruncal defects such as TOF, transposition of the great arteries, and interrupted aortic arch (type A). Additional associated abnormalities include right pulmonary artery origin from the aorta and anomalous coronary artery origin from the pulmonary artery.
paragraphs.heading: Associated Defects

paragraphs.text: Patients with an AP window are at increased risk of developing early pulmonary overcirculation and associated symptomatology, often in the first weeks of life. On examination, the precordium is hyperactive, second heart sound is usually single, and peripheral pulses are bounding.
paragraphs.heading: Clinical Presentation

paragraphs.text: Chest radiography often demonstrates cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings consistent with excessive pulmonary blood flow. Diagnosis is made by echocardiography. The location and size of the AP window are delineated, and special care must be taken to identify an associated PDA or interrupted arch, as well as coronary artery or branch pulmonary artery abnormalities.
paragraphs.heading: Diagnostic Evaluation

paragraphs.text: Surgical closure of an AP window is usually done shortly after diagnosis with excellent short- and long-term results.75 Delaying repair risks development of significant pulmonary arterial hypertension, potentially irreversible pulmonary vascular disease, and Eisenmenger syndrome. 76 Congenital Defects of the Cardiovascular System

### NATHANIEL ROBBINS AND JANINE ARRUDA

### Summary

Congenital heart defects are the most common type of birth defects worldwide. The following chapter provides an overview of the anatomy, physiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, and management strategies for a wide range of congenital heart disease in neonates and infants. Although the information herein is detailed, it is important to keep in mind that many different anatomic and physiologic variants are encountered in practice, often altering clinical management. The chapter is generally organized based on the predominant pathophysiology—cyanotic, obstructive, or shunting—for a given congenital heart defect. There can be considerable overlap between these physiologies, particularly in complex forms of congenital heart disease involving multiple defects. Defect physiology can also change considerably over time, particularly in the immediate postnatal transitional period around ductal closure. Prompt recognition and diagnosis of hemodynamically significant congenital heart defects can greatly impact effective management and outcomes in affected newborns and infants.

### Cyanotic Heart Defects: Mixing-Dependent

### Dextro-Transposition of the Great Arteries Anatomy and Pathophysiology

In dextro-transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA), the aorta arises from the right ventricle, which receives systemic venous deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricle, which receives pulmonary venous oxygenated blood. The blood flow in these patients is in parallel with the deoxygenated blood entering the aorta and recirculating to the body, while the richly oxygenated pulmonary venous return is recirculated to the lungs. In the absence of any shunting across connections between the systemic and pulmonary circulations to allow mixing of the deoxygenated and oxygenated blood, it results in systemic hypoxia and is often lethal. In D-TGA, three levels where

mixing can occur are atrial level defect (patent foramen ovale [PFO] or atrial septal defect [ASD]), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), or ventricular septal defect (VSD). The most effective site of mixing is at the atrial level through a PFO or ASD, with the other forms (PDA and VSD) being less reliable. It is therefore extremely important at birth to make sure that there is an adequately sized atrial level communication.

### Associated Defects

Associated defects have a dramatic effect on the presentation and pathophysiology of newborn infants with D-TGA. At a minimum, an atrial level defect with balanced bidirectional shunting is essential for survival. The presence of a PDA also allows for additional shunting from the aorta (deoxygenated blood) to the pulmonary artery (oxygenated blood), resulting in increased pulmonary venous return and added left-to-right shunting at the atrial level. An associated VSD occurs in about 25% of infants with D-TGA. Its presence contributes to mixing of the oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood, but, as previously stated, atrial level mixing is the most reliable. Coarctation of the aorta or aortic arch interruption can also occur in association with D-TGA, particularly in cases with a subpulmonary VSD.1

### Clinical Presentation

D-TGA is the most common cyanotic heart defect identified in the first week of life, and the diagnosis should be considered in any cyanotic neonate. Fetal diagnosis is common, and factors such as hypermobility of the atrial septum and reversal of diastolic flow in the PDA on fetal echocardiography can potentially predict the need for urgent balloon atrial septostomy.2 Even with prenatal diagnosis, however, profound hypoxia caused by a highly restrictive atrial level defect can lead to rapid deterioration and death within the first hours of life. Respiratory symptoms in this disorder are absent or limited to hyperpnea or tachypnea. The patient’s second heart sound is loud and single because of the anterior position of the aorta and

1411


## PDF page 1412

the posterior position of the pulmonary artery. A holosystolic murmur, when present, suggests an associated VSD; a systolic ejection murmur is auscultated in the setting of pulmonary stenosis (PS). In the absence of these associated defects, murmurs are generally not heard. The peripheral pulses are normal unless coarctation of the aorta is present. Persistent ductal patency or high pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) will affect the clinical findings of an associated VSD or coarctation of the aorta with potential for reverse differential cyanosis showing preductal saturation in the upper extremities lower than postductal saturation in the lower extremities.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

The electrocardiogram (ECG) is usually normal or may demonstrate right ventricular (RV) hypertrophy after a few weeks of life. Similarly, the classic egg-shaped heart with increased pulmonary vascularity on the chest radiograph might not be seen in the newborn period. Echocardiography defines the diagnosis, associated defects, and coronary artery anatomy, which are central to surgical planning.3 Cardiac catheterization is usually reserved for neonates requiring balloon atrial septostomy, and it is occasionally useful for further delineating other anatomic details, although it is rarely necessary to evaluate the coronary arteries (Fig. 76.1). Dual-source computed tomography angiography (CTA) can also be used for delineating coronary artery origin and course, as well as other associated intra- and extracardiac anomalies.4

### Management and Prognosis

Maintaining patency of the ductus arteriosus with intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion in newborn infants with D-TGA often improves arterial oxygenation by increasing shunting from the oxygen-rich pulmonary artery to the deoxygenated aorta. Aortic to pulmonary artery shunting at the ductal level may increase pulmonary venous return, distending the left atrium and facilitating left-to-right

History

Historically, the surgical interventions for D-TGA were the atrial switch operations, Senning (1959) and Mustard (1964). In these procedures, deoxygenated blood from the vena cavae is baffled to the morphologic left ventricle and then to the pulmonary artery, while the oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is directed to the morphologic right ventricle and the aorta. This results in physiologic circulation. However, the Senning and Mustard procedures are associated with a number of long-term complications, including RV dysfunction, systemic venous baffle obstruction and leaks, and atrial arrhythmias, as well as increased right atrial volumes and decreased right atrial emptying fractions.5

Arterial Switch Operation

Drs. Adib Jatene and Magdi Yacoub pioneered the anatomic repair of D-TGA via the arterial switch operation, which requires transection of the aorta and main pulmonary artery, reconnection to establish ventriculoarterial concordance (systemic left ventricle to the aorta and pulmonic right ventricle to the main pulmonary artery), and reimplantation of the coronary arteries to the neoaortic root. Other associated intracardiac defects are generally repaired at the time of the initial surgery. The arterial switch operation is optimally performed in the first week of life for infants with D-TGA. If there is a prolonged delay, the risk of left ventricular (LV) deconditioning and resultant inability to function adequately as the systemic ventricle increases. Long-term follow-up data on patients who have undergone the arterial switch operation are quite favorable.7 Risk factors for early mortality include prematurity, low birth weight, and RV hypoplasia. Abnormal coronary artery anatomy (particularly in cases with an intramural course), a risk factor in earlier experiences, can now be managed effectively, although with potentially higher hospital morbidity.6 Long-term follow-up studies demonstrate excellent ventricular function, normal rhythm, and low incidence of obstruction at the aortic and coronary suture lines. Narrowing in the supravalvar pulmonary area and branch pulmonary arteries may require subsequent surgeries or catheter interventions. Neoaortic root dilation and neoaortic valve regurgitation are found in some children, but these rarely require further intervention in childhood. Progressive neoaortic regurgitation requiring neoaortic valve replacement remains a long-term complication in adulthood.7 Follow-up data in children 16 years of age with D-TGA from the Boston Circulatory Arrest Study suggest that adolescents with D-TGA who have undergone the arterial switch operation are at increased

### Cyanotic Heart Defects: Restricted Pulmonary Blood Flow

### Tetralogy of Fallot Anatomy and Pathophysiology

In 1888, Etienne Fallot described the association of a large VSD, infundibular (subvalvar) and valvar PS, RV hypertrophy, and a large aorta overriding the ventricular septum—the tetralogy which bears his name. The spectrum of pulmonary lesions in tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) can range from mild PS with adequate oxygen saturation to pulmonary atresia with very low oxygen saturations. Infants with severe PS or atresia may have severely hypoplastic, discontinuous, or absent pulmonary arteries, with major aortopulmonary (AP) collateral arteries serving as the primary source of pulmonary blood flow. In TOF, cyanosis is proportional to the degree of right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction, with severe obstruction limiting pulmonary blood flow and leading to very low saturation. Shunting across the VSD is determined by an intricate balance between the systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). Hypercyanotic spells arise from acute worsening of RVOT narrowing or stenosis from the release of endogenous catecholamines, such as seen with agitation in a dehydrated infant, leading to increased PVR more than SVR, resulting in right-to-left shunting and worsening systemic desaturations.9

### Associated Defects

A right aortic arch is found in approximately 25% of patients with TOF.10 Coronary artery anomalies (e.g., left anterior descending coronary artery arising from the right coronary artery) are not uncommon and must be identified prior to surgical intervention.11 The branch pulmonary arteries may be stenotic or discontinuous with collateral supply from the aorta. Some patients also have multiple VSDs or ASDs, anomalous systemic venous drainage, or atrioventricular valve abnormalities. A rare, complex form is TOF with absent pulmonary valve, which results in pulmonary valve annulus hypoplasia, severe branch pulmonary artery dilation, significant bronchial compression, and airway abnormalities, including bronchomalacia.9 Up to 25% have associated chromosomal abnormalities with the most common being trisomy 21, 22q11.2 deletion, trisomy 18, and trisomy 13.12

### Clinical Presentation

The clinical presentation of TOF is directly related to the severity of RVOT obstruction. The intensely cyanotic newborn generally has severe PS or atresia with markedly diminished pulmonary blood flow and right-to-left shunting across the VSD. The minimally cyanotic or acyanotic infant

has a lesser degree of PS with mainly left-to-right shunting across the VSD. On exam, in neonates with TOF, the primary murmur is a systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border secondary to PS/RVOT obstruction. There may also be a single second heart sound due to marked decrease of its pulmonary component and a palpable RV impulse. The VSD in TOF is generally large and unrestrictive and does not produce a significant murmur. A continuous murmur may suggest systemic-to-pulmonary collaterals as the source of pulmonary blood flow.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

In the newborn with TOF, the classic finding on chest X-ray is a boot-shaped heart caused by RV hypertrophy and consequent upturned cardiac apex. The pulmonary vascular markings should also be carefully examined and may reflect the severity of RVOT obstruction. Echocardiography is the primary diagnostic tool and illustrates the anterior malalignment VSD resulting from anterior displacement of the conal septum leading to variable degrees of RVOT obstruction, RV hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta (Fig. 76.2). The levels and degrees of pulmonary obstruction and the size of the main and branch pulmonary arteries should be delineated, as well as other associated abnormalities, including coronary artery anomalies, additional VSDs, or collateral vessels.13 Presurgical diagnostic cardiac catheterization is only indicated if the pulmonary artery anatomy and pulmonary blood flow sources cannot be defined by noninvasive imaging modalities.14

### Management and Prognosis

Neonates with severe cyanosis in the immediate postnatal period are stabilized via intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus and increase pulmonary blood flow. In general, these neonates require a palliative systemic-to-pulmonary shunt (e.g., Blalock-Thomas-Taussig or central shunt) or complete

### Tricuspid Atresia Anatomy and Pathophysiology

In tricuspid atresia (TA), platelike tissue replaces the tricuspid valve, resulting in no direct communication between the right atrium and right ventricle. Systemic venous return from the vena cavae enters the right atrium and crosses the atrial septum with resultant complete mixing of the systemic and pulmonary venous return in the left atrium. Pulmonary blood flow is supplied by left-to-right shunting through either a PDA or VSD. Associated RV hypoplasia and pulmonary artery hypoplasia are proportional to the size of the VSD and the degree of subpulmonary stenosis and PS. The degree of hypoxemia is proportional to the relative systemic and pulmonary blood flows. Neonates with TA, a small VSD, and severe PS have severely limited pulmonary blood flow and are ductal dependent. Those with a large VSD and no PS have unrestrictive pulmonary blood flow, and, as the PVR falls, pulmonary blood flow dramatically increases with resultant signs and symptoms of pulmonary overcirculation, including feeding difficulties and growth failure.

### Associated Defects

All neonates with TA must have an atrial level defect for postnatal survival. Other associated lesions include VSD, TGA, atrioventricular septal defect, and aortic coarctation. The VSD size is extremely important in neonates with TA and TGA, as oxygenated blood flows through the VSD into the right ventricle and then the aorta. Restriction of blood flow through the VSD can compromise flow to the aorta and the systemic circulation.

### Clinical Presentation

The typical neonatal presentation of TA is cyanosis at or before ductal closure in an infant with a murmur. Precordial activity is normal, and the second heart sound is often

single. There may be a systolic ejection murmur if there is RVOT obstruction. If the VSD is large, tachypnea, a LV impulse, and a third heart sound may develop during the first few days of life as the PVR falls. Hepatic enlargement is an indicator of a restrictive ASD and elevated right atrial pressures.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

The ECG is usually diagnostic in neonates with TA, demonstrating right atrial enlargement and left-axis deviation. The chest radiograph tends to be nonspecific, although in severely cyanotic neonates it may show decreased pulmonary vascularity. The echocardiogram (Fig. 76.3) clearly defines the anatomy, in addition to abnormalities of the great arteries or aortic coarctation. Diagnosis as well as associated anatomical defects can be accurately identified prenatally by fetal echocardiography.19 Heart catheterization may be performed for balloon atrial septostomy in those with a restrictive atrial septum.

### Management and Prognosis

Flow across the VSD to supply the pulmonary circulation may be adequate in the first months of life as long as the atrial level defect remains unrestrictive. It is generally possible to predict by echocardiogram when infants require a PDA to maintain adequate arterial saturations. A balloon atrial septostomy is rarely necessary unless there is significant restriction at the atrial level. Off bypass surgical septostomy on the beating heart has been used in rare cases.20 If a newborn is deemed ductal dependent or if hypoxia increases in the first month of life, a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt is necessary to provide adequate pulmonary blood flow and oxygenation. Conversion to a bidirectional cavopulmonary (Glenn shunt) anastomosis is usually considered between 3 and 6 months of age. Some infants with well-balanced systemic and pulmonary flows can proceed directly to an early bidirectional Glenn operation followed by a total cavopulmonary (Fontan operation) connection at about 2 to 3 years of age.21 Although nearly 10% of children will not reach Fontan completion, among children who undergo the Fontan type of operation those with TA have an excellent long-term prognosis, with a low prevalence of ventricular dysfunction, mitral regurgitation, arrhythmias, and systemic venous congestion.22

The pulmonary valve in pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (PA/IVS) can range from a well-formed pulmonary annulus with a plate or membrane that obstructs outflow to a completely underdeveloped valve. All forms may lead to severe RV hypertrophy, RV dysfunction, and variable degrees of RV hypoplasia. Because the ventricular septum is intact, pulmonary blood flow in PA/IVS is ductal dependent and can only occur via shunting at the level of the atria and PDA. ### Associated Defects

A very important prognostic feature in PA/IVS concerns the presence or absence of ventriculocoronary connections (sinusoids and fistulae) and coronary artery abnormalities. These must be well defined prior to surgical or transcatheter intervention. In the case of RV-dependent coronary circulation, where coronary artery flow depends on high RV pressures for adequate myocardial perfusion, decompressing the RV can lead to untoward consequences such as myocardial ischemia, infarction, and death. ### Clinical Presentation

Fetal diagnosis of PA/IVS frequently identifies risk factors for subsequent transcatheter and surgical management, including tricuspid valve and RV hypoplasia, coronary sinusoids, and fistulae.24 Neonates with PA/IVS develop severe hypoxemia as the ductus arteriosus closes and can rapidly become unstable with tachypnea, tachycardia, hepatomegaly, and cardiorespiratory collapse. Cyanosis becomes apparent within hours of birth and is progressive. Tachypnea may be prominent. First and second heart sounds are single, and there may be a holosystolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border consistent with tricuspid regurgitation. A PDA murmur may be audible, particularly following initiation of prostaglandin infusion. Unless there is severe tricuspid regurgitation or a restrictive atrial communication,

the liver generally is not enlarged while ductal patency is maintained.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

Chest radiography in PA/IVS often shows cardiomegaly due to right atrial enlargement. Echocardiography is diagnostic, demonstrating the pulmonary valve atresia, tricuspid valve abnormalities, degree of RV hypoplasia, and coronary anomalies, including sinusoids and findings suggestive of coronary fistulae. Cardiac catheterization is indicated to assess coronary flow, the presence (including size and location) or absence of coronary sinusoids and fistulae, and pulmonary blood flow sources, as well as for consideration of pulmonary valve intervention.

### Management and Prognosis

Intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion is essential for maintaining ductal patency in PA/IVS. Careful assessment of the anatomy and physiology provides a framework for transcatheter consideration and surgical management.25 Balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty is feasible in infants with even a diminutive pulmonary valve orifice, and other transcatheter techniques, including radiofrequency perforation of the valve, may be considered. Although still in the early experience and offered at only a few centers, fetal intervention to perforate the pulmonary valve can allow for future biventricular repair in patients who otherwise would have been univentricular repair candidates. Perventricular pulmonary valve perforation has also allowed for successful RV decompression.26

If interventional catheterization is unsuccessful, surgical valvotomy can be performed unless RV-dependent coronary circulation is present. In these circumstances, RV decompression can result in coronary hypoperfusion; therefore a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt is recommended as initial palliation to provide pulmonary blood flow. In infants who have undergone successful surgical or transcatheter valvotomies, RV growth is possible and biventricular circulation can be restored. Severe tricuspid and RV hypoplasia or RVdependent coronary circulation are indications for single ventricle palliation.25 Infants with RV hypoplasia should also be considered candidates for superior cavopulmonary (Glenn) anastomosis combined with closure of the atrial level defect (the so-called 1.5 ventricle repair). This results in a direction of inferior vena cava flow across the tricuspid valve into the RV, promoting potential RV growth.

In particular, the septal leaflet can become tethered to the interventricular septum to varying degrees with apical displacement of its annular attachment, potentially leading to significant tricuspid regurgitation. The anterior tricuspid leaflet can also become markedly enlarged and redundant (“sail-like”), causing RVOT obstruction with decreased

Secondary to apical tricuspid annular displacement into the right ventricle, a portion of the RV becomes atrialized, detrimentally affecting its contractile efficiency.27 Forward pulmonary blood flow is therefore dependent on the severity of tricuspid valve displacement and regurgitation and RV atrialization and dysfunction. If functional or anatomic pulmonary atresia occurs, an obligatory right-toleft shunt must exist at the atrial level, and its degree is proportional to the severity of the tricuspid valve abnormality.28

### Associated Defects

Patients with Ebstein anomaly often have other associated intracardiac lesions, including the aforementioned pulmonary atresia and atrial level defects. Conduction system abnormalities such as accessory pathways (e.g., Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) are found in up to 20% of cases.28

### Clinical Presentation

Infants with severe Ebstein anomaly may present with profound cyanosis, tachypnea, and cardiovascular collapse. Cyanosis is dependent on the extent of atrial right-to-left shunting. A low-frequency holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation is often heard, and the first heart sound may be widely split.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

The ECG of infants with severe Ebstein anomaly often shows an rSr′ pattern in the right precordial leads, suggesting RV dilation. Chest radiography can demonstrate severe cardiomegaly caused by right atrial dilation. Echocardiography helps delineate the extent of tricuspid valve displacement, atrial level shunting, and functional or anatomic pulmonary atresia. The ratio of the right atrial plus atrialized RV size to the functional RV plus left heart (left atrium and ventricle) size has been utilized as a measure of severity and outcome. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows for volumetric and functional measurements of the right ventricle, and serial assessments can be used for monitoring of disease progression.29

### Management and Prognosis

Mild forms of Ebstein anomaly require no specific treatment early on, and infants in general do well. The severely affected neonate with severe tricuspid valve apical displacement and regurgitation is often ductal dependent with minimal or no anterograde flow across the pulmonary valve.28 Maintaining ductal patency with prostaglandin E1 infusion can be useful in the short term; however, ductal flow into the pulmonary artery can make antegrade flow more difficult. In severe Ebstein anomaly, measures to lower the PVR, including nitric oxide, and attempts to wean prostaglandin E1 might be necessary before anterograde flow across the pulmonary valve can be established. Brief support with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation to facilitate fetal-to-neonatal transition has been successful in limited cases. Surgical repair or replacement of the valve is feasible and may be indicated

in older children, but it is not useful in neonates. Either transplantation or surgical exclusion of the right ventricle, with plans for a long-term, single-ventricle palliation might be the only alternatives for the neonate with severe Ebstein anomaly and persistent cyanosis.30

### Cyanotic Heart Defects: Complete Mixing

### Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection/Return Anatomy and Pathophysiology

Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection or return (TAPVC/TAPVR) comprises a group of defects in which all of the pulmonary veins carrying oxygenated blood drain into the systemic venous circulation rather than normally to the left atrium. A number of distinct variants have been identified:



Supracardiac type—In its most common form, an ascending

vertical vein emanates from the pulmonary venous confluence posterior to the left atrium and connects to the left innominate vein, which then drains to the superior vena cava (SVC) and right atrium. Infracardiac type—A descending vertical vein emanates from

the pulmonary venous confluence posterior to the left atrium and courses inferiorly, crossing through the diaphragm and the liver with variable drainage to the ductus venosus, hepatic veins, portal vein, or inferior vena cava with obstruction at one or more of these sites and eventual pulmonary venous drainage to the right atrium. Cardiac type—Pulmonary veins drain to the right atrium via

an intracardiac connection, generally the coronary sinus, or directly to the right atrium. Mixed type—Anomalous pulmonary venous connections

occur at two or more levels. Typically, the left pulmonary veins may drain into the systemic veins through an ascending vertical vein (supracardiac), and the right pulmonary veins drain into the coronary sinus or directly into the right atrium (cardiac). Other complex variants have been reported as well (Fig. 76.4).

The supracardiac form is most common, occurring in roughly half of cases, and the mixed form is the least common. Infracardiac TAPVC in particular may present in extremis in the neonatal period due to obstruction of the descending vertical vein at the diaphragm, the ductus venosus, or the portal vein. The supracardiac form less commonly presents with obstruction when the vertical vein passes between the left bronchus and the left pulmonary artery or at the junction of the SVC and the innominate vein. In TAPVC, oxygenated pulmonary venous return mixes completely with deoxygenated systemic venous flow in the right atrium. Systemic blood flow is dependent on the obligatory shunting from the right atrium to the left atrium through an atrial level defect. Cyanosis and respiratory distress are generally seen in infants with the severe forms of obstructed pulmonary venous connections or restrictive atrial communications. In infants without obstruction, volume overload, increased pulmonary blood flow, and inadequate weight gain gradually develop.

Chest radiography is very helpful in TAPVC, as pulmonary edema is highly suggestive of pulmonary venous obstruction. ### Truncus Arteriosus Anatomy and Pathophysiology

In truncus arteriosus, the brachiocephalic, pulmonary, and coronary arteries arise from a single arterial trunk. This single trunk overrides a large VSD that allows mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous return. In type I, a short main pulmonary artery segment arises from the truncus arteriosus, and it gives rise to the branch pulmonary arteries. In type II, both branch pulmonary arteries have a direct origin from the common trunk. In type III, the pulmonary arteries arise from opposite sides of the common truncus and are remote from each other. Truncus arteriosus with the absence of one pulmonary artery branch and the presence of major AP artery collateral arteries are rare forms.34 Both pulmonary and systemic blood flows are determined by the relative SVRs and PVRs. As the PVR falls, there tends to be increased pulmonary blood flow, resulting in pulmonary overcirculation and increased left atrial and ventricular size.

### Associated Defects

A number of other cardiac defects are seen in association with truncus arteriosus. Importantly, the single semilunar truncal valve is often thickened and dysplastic and demonstrates variable morphology, with anywhere from one to six leaflets and differing degrees of valvar stenosis and regurgitation. Unilateral or bilateral branch pulmonary artery stenosis occurs in about 10% of cases. Coronary artery anomalies and stenosis are rare but are surgically important variations.35 A right aortic arch is found in 15% to 25% of patients with truncus arteriosus, and aortic coarctation or interrupted aortic arch may also be present. In addition, 22q11 chromosomal microdeletion (DiGeorge) syndrome is a very common association, and genetic testing should be obtained.

### Clinical Presentation

The neonatal presentation of uncomplicated truncus arteriosus can be subtle, with mild tachypnea and/or cyanosis as the only symptom. Systemic oxygen saturation is generally in the mid-80% range, and it increases as PVR drops and pulmonary blood flow increases. Lower saturation may indicate increased PVR, branch pulmonary artery stenosis, or pulmonary edema. Acidosis can be present in infants with associated truncal stenosis and regurgitation or aortic arch obstruction. As the PVR drops, pulmonary blood flow increases, resulting in signs and symptoms of pulmonary overcirculation. Truncal valve stenosis and regurgitation murmurs can be identified on exam. Infants may have bounding peripheral

pulses and increased pulse pressures secondary to decreased diastolic pressure caused by blood flow runoff into the branch pulmonary arteries. Poor perfusion and decreased leg pulses may indicate aortic coarctation or arch interruption. Given the association with 22q11 chromosomal microdeletion syndrome and absent thymus, serum calcium should be monitored in all patients with truncus arteriosus.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

Chest radiography in truncus arteriosus typically demonstrates cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vasculature markings. An ECG may show biventricular hypertrophy or be normal. Echocardiography is the gold standard for diagnosis—attention must be paid to define the truncal valve anatomy and function, branch pulmonary arteries, aortic arch anatomy, and coronary arteries. Cardiac catheterization, CTA, and MRI are reserved for cases where the anatomy has not been well defined by echocardiography. Chromosomal microarray testing should be obtained in all infants with truncus arteriosus.

### Management and Prognosis

In infants with truncus arteriosus, symptoms related to increased pulmonary blood flow generally respond well to diuretics and digoxin. Supplemental oxygen should be avoided, as it decreases PVR, increasing pulmonary blood flow. Infants with moderate to severe truncal valve stenosis or regurgitation generally do not respond well to medical management and may require transcatheter balloon valvuloplasty or early surgical intervention. In 22q11 infants, careful management of calcium levels is required. Truncus arteriosus is typically repaired in the first months of life, and it consists of patch closure of VSD and placement of a right ventricle to pulmonary artery (RV-PA) conduit. Associated defects, including truncal valve stenosis, aortic arch interruption, coronary abnormalities, and branch pulmonary artery atresia, may increase procedural risk but do not preclude it.36 If truncal valve stenosis or regurgitation is severe, surgical replacement may be indicated to provide a competent neoaortic valve. The long-term prognosis for infants with uncomplicated repaired truncus arteriosus is excellent. RV-PA conduit replacement is generally needed by age 5 years in about 20% of patients, and a lifetime of multiple surgical and transcatheter replacements is required. The truncal/neoaortic valve may develop worsening stenosis and can require valve repair or replacement in 25% of patients. Interventions on the RV outflow and pulmonary arteries are performed in over half of these patients at 20 years following their initial operation.37 Ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmias are generally poor prognostic indicators.

### Single Ventricle Anatomy/Physiology

Congenital heart disease resulting in single ventricle anatomy or physiology encompasses a wide range of defects

Furthermore, basic physiologic principles help guide management in this population. For example, there must be adequate mixing of systemic and pulmonary venous return to support single ventricular output. This mixing occurs most effectively through an atrial level defect (PFO or ASD). Additional shunting and mixing can also occur via a VSD or PDA. The single ventricle predominantly pumps blood to either the systemic or pulmonary circulation, and the predominant circulation must then support the other via shunting through a PDA. Systemic oxygen saturations are determined by the relative resistances across the pulmonary and systemic vascular beds. It is important to recognize that many infants have low PVR, resulting in unrestrictive pulmonary blood flow. Oxygen acts as a pulmonary vasodilator, further increasing pulmonary blood flow, often at the cost of systemic blood flow, and therefore should be used judiciously.

When single ventricle anatomy/physiology has been diagnosed, the next step is to determine whether the pulmonary or systemic circulation requires support. This primarily guides the interventions needed for effective management, including long-term surgical planning. Advances in fetal echocardiography have allowed for increased prenatal diagnosis, better expectant management, and collaborative work among obstetrics, pediatric cardiology, intensive care, and cardiothoracic surgery teams to optimize care for these patients and better prepare the affected families for the challenges ahead.

### Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome

Before 1980, no effective palliation was available for infants with hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). Staged surgical palliation, including the Norwood operation with its modifications,38 and neonatal cardiac transplantation have offered new hope to the families of newborn infants with this otherwise uniformly lethal cardiac defect. Advances in both approaches have greatly improved the duration and quality of life for these patients.

### Anatomy and Pathophysiology

HLHS consists of a spectrum of congenital abnormalities of the mitral and aortic valves, ranging from mitral stenosis and aortic stenosis to mitral atresia and aortic atresia in the most severe variants. It then results in variable degrees of LV hypoplasia and ascending aorta and aortic arch hypoplasia. Aortic coarctation may be present, and LV endocardial fibroelastosis can result from in utero subendocardial ischemia. Coronary artery abnormalities have also been identified but have uncertain impact on long-term myocardial function. In HLHS, the systemic circulation is ductal dependent— ductal flow courses retrograde to the transverse arch and ascending aorta to supply the brachiocephalic vessels and coronary arteries, as well as antegrade to the descending

aorta. In utero, when PVR is high, this circulation provides excellent organ perfusion, and fetal growth is usually normal. Postnatally, even as PVR falls and pulmonary blood flow increases, RV output remains adequate to supply both the systemic and pulmonary circulations. However, ductal closure dramatically alters this balance, leading to profound systemic and myocardial hypoperfusion with metabolic acidosis and multisystem organ failure.

### Associated Defects

The most important associated intracardiac defect in HLHS is an unrestrictive atrial level shunt. An absent or restrictive atrial defect in utero creates severe pulmonary venous hypertension, leading to detrimental pulmonary vasculature changes. Significant atrial restriction can result in greatly increased morbidity and mortality in the neonatal period and is a major negative prognostic factor in postnatal outcomes, particularly in the subgroup with mitral or aortic atresia. Fetal diagnosis also allows for consideration of fetal atrial septoplasty or atrial stent implantation in the select patient with a restrictive atrial septum.39,62 Other important associated defects for HLHS include pulmonary venous return anomalies. Occasional neonates with aortic atresia may have a normal-sized mitral valve and left ventricle because of an associated VSD. Central nervous system anomalies, including absent corpus callosum, are also quite common in infants with HLHS. Furthermore, there is increasing recognition of the in utero effects of congenital heart disease, including HLHS, on prenatal brain development and postnatal neurodevelopmental outcomes.40

### Clinical Presentation

Increasing prenatal diagnosis of HLHS has greatly helped prepare families and improve coordination between the medical teams involved in the delivery and initial management of these infants. Infants with HLHS often have tachypnea and mild cyanosis in the postnatal period. There can be a moderately increased RV impulse on exam, a single second heart sound, and variable murmurs. With ductal patency, pulses can be nearly normal. Pulse oximetry varies widely, ranging from 70% to greater than 90%, depending on the amount of pulmonary blood flow and degree of pulmonary edema. A restrictive atrial level defect can produce significant pulmonary edema because of increased left atrial pressure and resultant increased pulmonary venous pressure. The combination of pulmonary edema and restricted pulmonary blood flow produces profound hypoxia.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

The ECG in HLHS generally demonstrates dominant RV forces, often with a QR pattern in the right chest leads. Chest radiography shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary blood flow with more prominent pulmonary vascular markings and pulmonary venous congestion. Echocardiography (Fig. 76.5) defines the underlying anatomy, including the atrial level defect and its degree of restriction, atrioventricular valve regurgitation, ventricular function, outflow tract

### Management and Prognosis

In HLHS, the systemic circulation is ductal dependent, and maintaining ductal patency in the immediate postnatal period with intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion is critical for survival. In patients with a severely restrictive ASD, balloon atrial septostomy can be performed to reduce pulmonary venous pressure and pulmonary edema.41 Beyond this period, a staged surgical approach is used in most centers. Neonatal cardiac transplantation42 remains an option but is greatly limited by donor heart availability. A hybrid approach combined with ventricular assist device insertion can be used as a bridge to transplantation in suboptimal candidates for Norwood palliation.43 No matter the chosen strategy, careful postnatal assessment and management to prevent complications from excessive pulmonary blood flow are essential for good long-term results. The overall goal of staged surgical palliation for HLHS is to separate the systemic and pulmonary circulations in a stepwise fashion while ensuring adequate systemic blood flow at each stage and protecting the pulmonary vasculature from excessive flow and pulmonary hypertension. Surgical and interventional techniques in addition to postsurgical management have evolved greatly over a number of decades to address the various issues that have been recognized during the evolution of the current staged approach.

In most centers, initial (stage I) surgical palliation is done in the immediate postnatal period with a Norwood

procedure, including aortic reconstruction, systemic-topulmonary arterial shunt placement (modified Blalock- Thomas-Taussig [mBTT] shunt or RV-PA conduit [Sano modification]), and atrial septectomy. A Damus-Kaye- Stansel anastomosis may be utilized if the ascending aorta is of sufficient size.44 Stage I palliation may also be accomplished via a hybrid procedure done by surgical and interventional catheterization teams working in tandem. Hybrid stage I palliation consists of surgical bilateral branch pulmonary artery banding and transcatheter PDA stent placement. The theoretical advantages of this approach are avoidance of cardiopulmonary bypass and circulatory arrest (and their potential associated adverse effects) in the neonatal period and delay of major aortic intervention/reconstruction to an older age when infants are larger. This approach can be complicated by the need for ongoing catheter interventions on branch pulmonary arteries following subsequent staged surgeries.45 The primary goals of both Norwood and hybrid stage I palliation are to provide adequate systemic blood flow and to effectively control pulmonary blood flow. Postoperative management requires very close monitoring of systemic perfusion and appropriate cardiovascular and respiratory support as needed to avoid tissue/organ hypoxia. Typical systemic arterial saturations following stage I palliation are in the mid-70% to mid-80% range. Even with greatly improved surgical and intensive care techniques, a proportion of infants after stage I palliation require extracorporeal membrane oxygenation support to achieve stability with eventual poor results.46,62

Following either stage I technique, stage II palliation entails completing a superior cavopulmonary (Glenn shunt) anastomosis or hemi-Fontan procedure to allow the SVC flow to directly drain into the pulmonary arteries.47 In the hybrid approach, the previously deferred aortic reconstruction must also be completed, and the total operation is denoted a comprehensive stage II procedure. Stage II palliation is typically completed between 4 and 6 months of age and results in systemic venous return from the upper body (via the SVC) as the sole source of pulmonary blood flow. Because SVC flow no longer drains to the systemic single ventricle, the ventricular volume loading is reduced, lessening its overall workload and reducing the potential for ventricular dysfunction. Typical systemic arterial saturations following stage II palliation climb into the mid-70% to mid-80% range.

Staged surgical palliation for HLHS is completed at approximately 2 to 4 years of age via a total cavopulmonary connection (Fontan procedure) to direct inferior vena cava drainage to the pulmonary arteries. ### Double Outlet Right Ventricle Anatomy and Pathophysiology

In double outlet right ventricle (DORV), the aorta and the pulmonary artery both arise from the right ventricle. There are four distinct subtypes based on the location of the VSD and its relationship to the great arteries: (1) subaortic, (2) subpulmonary, (3) doubly committed, or (4) remote from the great arteries. The Taussig-Bing malformation is a DORV variant with a subpulmonary VSD and D-malposition of the aorta, typically side-by-side with the pulmonary artery. DORV physiology is determined

by VSD location and associated defects, ranging from excessive pulmonary blood flow from a large VSD shunt physiology to transposition physiology due to streaming of blood flow.

### Associated Defects

Commonly associated defects in DORV are subvalvar and/ or valvar PS. In DORV with a subaortic VSD and PS, the physiology is similar to TOF. In the Taussig-Bing variant where the blood flow is preferentially directed toward the pulmonary artery, associated aortic arch anomalies, including coarctation or interruption, are often seen.

### Clinical Presentation

The clinical presentation of DORV in the neonatal period can vary widely and include significant cyanosis in transposition variants or when there is associated severe PS or atresia, or shock and cardiovascular collapse with ductal closure in Taussig-Bing variants with coarctation of the aorta or interrupted aortic arch. As the PVR drops, tachypnea may develop if pulmonary blood flow is unrestricted. A murmur generally suggests the presence of PS, which may protect the pulmonary vascular bed and result in a well-balanced circulation with mild cyanosis.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

The ECG and chest radiograph in DORV are nonspecific. Echocardiography is used to delineate its features, including VSD location, size, and relationship to the great arteries. The great artery configuration and relationship to each other, the presence of PS, and aortic arch abnormalities should be easily identified.

### Management and Prognosis

Surgical intervention for DORV is dependent on the predominant physiology, as well as VSD location and its relationship to the great arteries and associated lesions. Hence, definitive repair could simply entail VSD closure or become increasingly complex to involve components such as an arterial switch operation or coarctation/interrupted arch repair, or the need for initial systemic-to-pulmonary artery shunt followed by right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery conduit later in infancy.52 DORV repair is generally performed in the first 6 months of life.

IAA and hemodynamically significant aortic coarctation result in systemic hypertension, increased LV afterload, and LV hypertrophy. Severe aortic obstruction from a severe coarctation or IAA can lead to LV failure and inadequate perfusion distal to the obstruction, particularly with ductal closure. Thus maintenance of ductal patency is critical to survival and well-being in these infants prior to intervention. Conversely, a significant coarctation may be unmasked during ductal closure. Aside from effects on the LV myocardium, neonatal coarctation may also affect the RV myocardium due to LV diastolic dysfunction, pulmonary venous congestion, pulmonary hypertension, and interventricular interactions, leading to RV hypertrophy and dysfunction.

The most common defects associated with aortic coarctation are bicuspid aortic valve (50% to almost 85% of cases in some series) and VSD. Mitral valve anomalies may also be present. IAA is commonly associated with posterior malalignment VSD resulting in subaortic stenosis. Other associated lesions include AP window, truncus arteriosus, and transposition of the great arteries. Both aortic coarctation and IAA may complicate other forms of complex congenital heart disease. With regard to genetic disorders, aortic coarctation has a known association with Turner syndrome, and IAA can be seen with partial or complete 22q11 chromosomal microdeletion syndrome, particularly in the setting of a right aortic arch.

Mild aortic coarctation with no associated valvar aortic stenosis or VSD is generally asymptomatic. Infants will often have diminished femoral pulses on exam but no other outward signs or symptoms. The hallmarks of significant arch obstruction are diminished femoral pulses and blood pressure and oxygen saturation differentials between the upper and lower extremities, although all these may be less pronounced in the setting of dysfunction. Careful assessment of all peripheral pulses can be valuable. Blood pressure should be measured on all four extremities to evaluate for discrepancies. Tachycardia, precordial hyperactivity, single second heart sound, a gallop rhythm, and hepatomegaly are markers of significant obstruction and possible associated defects. The typical systolic murmur of aortic coarctation—most prominent over the left infraclavicular region and under the left scapula—is well appreciated in older children with coarctation but may not be heard in neonates.

The ECG of a neonate with aortic coarctation or IAA may demonstrate LV hypertrophy. Chest radiographs are usually normal. Significant cardiomegaly suggests associated lesions or ventricular dilation or dysfunction following ductal closure. Ascertaining coarctation severity in the presence of a sizable PDA can be difficult, as the aortic isthmus may be surrounded by ductal tissue. ### Valvar Pulmonary Stenosis Anatomy and Pathophysiology

Isolated neonatal valvar pulmonary stenosis (PS) most commonly results from dysplasia of the valve leaflets with resultant thickening and decreased mobility, leading to varying degrees of obstruction at the valvar level. Associated RV hypertension and hypertrophy occur in proportion to obstruction severity. Post-stenotic main pulmonary artery dilation is also commonly found. The direction of atrial and ventricular level shunts, when present, is usually determined by the degree of RV hypertension and RV compliance.

### Associated Defects

The most commonly associated abnormality with PS is fixed or dynamic subvalvar (infundibular) narrowing or stenosis. Murmur intensity correlates with obstruction severity. In moderate to severe PS, an increased RV impulse may be noted.

### Management and Prognosis

The natural history of isolated valvar PS is excellent. In mild cases, most studies demonstrate minimal progression and spontaneous resolution in the majority of cases. However, up to a third of patients in some series may progress to moderate or severe levels of obstruction, typically in the first 6 months to 1 year of life. Transcatheter pulmonary balloon valvuloplasty is indicated for severe PS, and the timing is determined by the RVOT/ pulmonary valve gradient, degree of RV hypertrophy, or presence of RV dysfunction by echocardiography. ### Shunting Lesions

### Ventricular Septal Defect Anatomy and Pathophysiology

Ventricular septation is a complex embryologic process involving the development and fusion of the muscular ventricular septum, membranous area, conal or outlet septum, and atrioventricular endocardial cushions to form the interventricular septum. Abnormalities in this process result in VSDs, which are the most common forms of congenital heart defects, making up 20% of identified lesions in some population studies. They are classified according to their anatomic location: perimembranous, muscular, inlet, or malalignment or conal septal defects. Perimembranous VSDs are the most common, representing approximately 80% of cases. The amount of shunting through these defects is determined by their size, number, and relative PVRs and SVRs. In the immediate neonatal period, when PVR and RV pressures are high, left-to-right flow may be limited. However, with normal postnatal physiologic transition, PVR falls significantly over the first hours to days of life, with continued gradual decrease toward adult levels within the first 6 to 8 weeks. This results in lower RV pressures and increased left-to-right shunting. With sizable defects, signs and symptoms of pulmonary overcirculation develop, leading to left atrial and LV enlargement.

### Associated Defects

VSDs are often present in more complex forms of congenital heart disease, including many of the lesions discussed in

this chapter. Their location, size, and number can affect the presentation and clinical course of other associated lesions such as D-TGA, DORV, and coarctation of the aorta.

### Clinical Presentation

VSDs can be identified by a characteristic holosystolic murmur usually best heard at the left lower sternal border, generated by the left-to-right shunt through the defect. The pitch and duration of the murmur are determined by the size, location of the VSD, and pressure differences between the LV and RV. The common small, pressure-restrictive perimembranous VSD will produce a harsh holosystolic murmur and a possible palpable thrill. A murmur from a small muscular defect may be softer and short as the left-to-right shunt ceases during ventricular systole when surrounded by muscle. Larger VSDs can be more difficult to identify in the immediate postnatal period, given the elevated PVR and less disturbed shunt flow in the setting of nearly equal LV and RV pressures. Similarly, clinical evidence of significant left-toright shunting and resultant pulmonary overcirculation may not become apparent until the PVR drops after the immediate neonatal period. Many newborns with isolated VSDs are discharged home with no symptoms and may not be diagnosed until the initial outpatient followup visits.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

Smaller VSDs are routinely diagnosed with careful clinical examination, given their characteristic murmur location and quality. Anatomic type, size, number, direction of blood flow, mechanisms of closure such as surrounding tricuspid valve tissue, or aortic valve prolapse and associated defects are well defined by echocardiography.

### Management and Prognosis

Most VSDs require no intervention and undergo spontaneous closure within the first few months to years of life, particularly small to medium perimembranous and muscular defects. These are usually hemodynamically insignificant, and patients remain asymptomatic. Larger VSDs of any type can result in considerable left-to-right shunting, signs and symptoms of pulmonary overcirculation including tachypnea, increased work of breathing, diaphoresis with feedings, feeding difficulties, and suboptimal weight gain. These symptoms in association with LV enlargement are indications for initiation of oral diuretics to help reduce pulmonary symptoms and to improve feedings and growth. Exposure to long-term significant left-to-right shunting can lead to maladaptive pulmonary vascular changes and increased risks for development of pulmonary vaso-occlusive disease. Indications for surgical VSD closure include persistent respiratory symptoms, frequent respiratory infections despite anticongestive therapy, inadequate growth despite optimized nutrition and medical therapy, evidence of pulmonary hypertension, aortic valve leaflet prolapse, development and progression

### Atrial Septal Defect

Similar to ventricular septation, embryologic atrial septation is complex, and derangements in the process can result in abnormal interatrial communications. ASDs are classified according to their location and embryologic origin. The major types of ASDs are ostium secundum, ostium primum, and sinus venosus (SVC and IVC types); also, although coronary sinus defects are not truly ASDs, they result in left-to-right shunts and are often included in the classification. Secundum ASDs are the most common, representing over two-thirds of cases. Primum ASDs are a component of atrioventricular septal defects, and sinus venosus ASDs can be associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return. Isolated secundum ASDs diagnosed during the neonatal period are generally an incidental finding, and differentiating small defects from stretched foramen ovale can be challenging. True secundum ASDs including large defects rarely cause symptoms in neonates and infants when isolated and in the absence of comorbidities such as prematurity and its related respiratory complications. Isolated small to moderate secundum ASDs often close spontaneously over time. However, more sizable secundum ASDs must be longitudinally monitored, as they lead to right heart enlargement and may have to be closed during the preschool age, usually between 4 and 6 years of age. When amenable, transcatheter ASD device occlusion has become the preferred approach, with excellent results in children.65

### Atrioventricular Septal Defect Anatomy and Pathophysiology

Atrioventricular canal defects (AVCDs) represent a spectrum of abnormalities resulting from failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse during embryologic cardiac development. The most severe form is a complete AVCD, consisting of an ostium primum ASD, inlet VSD, and common AV valve. Other commonly seen variants include partial AVCD (ostium primum ASD with a cleft mitral valve) and transitional AVCD (ostium primum ASD, cleft mitral valve, and small inlet VSD). The pathophysiology of any AVCD variant depends on the size of the defects and resultant shunting. For example, the physiology of a partial or transitional AVCD mirrors that of a simple ASD, as the majority of shunting occurs at the atrial level. The physiology of a complete AVCD, with sizeable atrial and ventricular septal defects on the other hand, combines ASD and VSD physiology and significant volume overload. These lesions are rarely symptomatic in the immediate neonatal period in the absence of other defects or conditions.

### Associated Defects

The common AV valve in AVCD is often structurally abnormal, and varying degrees of regurgitation are common. Common AV valve abnormalities may also cause unbalanced ventricular development, leading to right- or left-ventricular dominance. In more extreme cases, this produces single ventricle anatomy and physiology. A common atrium with near complete absence of the atrial septum can be found in some variants, and associated systemic and pulmonary venous anomalies may also be present in the more complex forms. Complete AV canal defects can be seen in association with TOF and DORV, and it is seen in 20% to 30% of trisomy 21 patients.66

### Clinical Presentation

Significant common AV valve regurgitation can be appreciated as a holosystolic murmur at the apex on exam. It can lead to pulmonary venous congestion and pulmonary edema and can present with tachypnea and increased work of breathing. The large ostium primum ASD and inlet VSD components of the complete atrioventricular canal do not tend to produce significant or characteristic murmurs, particularly in the immediate postnatal period when the PVR is elevated, limiting the extra pulmonary blood flow from the large left-to-right shunts. Systemic oxygen saturation tends to be normal, and cyanosis is generally seen in more complex variants, such as the unbalanced forms with single ventricle physiology or associated TOF.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

The ECG in neonates with AVCD can be characteristic with significant left-axis deviation and right atrial enlargement. The axis deviation results from displacement of the conduction pathways away from their usual locations because of the intracardiac defects. The AVCD type, the atrial and ventricular component sizes, ventricular balance, AV valve morphology and function, outflow tracts, and associated lesions are all well defined by echocardiography.

### Management and Prognosis

A balanced, complete AVCD with no significant common AV valve abnormalities, ventricular dysfunction, or outflow tract anomalies is usually electively repaired during the first 4 to 6 months of life with a high degree of success.67 Infants with trisomy 21 sometimes undergo earlier repair because of the potential for early development of significant pulmonary hypertension. Following complete repair, long-term issues primarily involve AV valve function (stenosis or regurgitation) and development of LV outflow tract obstruction due to accessory AV valve tissue or more complex mechanisms. Infants with partial AV canal defects and no significant MV insufficiency can often wait until the preschool years for complete surgical repair. When more significant MV insufficiency, respiratory symptoms, or growth issues are present, surgical repair is recommended at an earlier age.
