### Anatomy and Pathophysiology

The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta in utero, and it is essential during fetal life. Given the high fetal PVR, only 10% to 15% of blood ejected by the right ventricle goes to the lungs, and the remaining flows through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta. The ductus arteriosus generally undergoes spontaneous closure in the immediate postnatal period, and the entire RV output is then ejected into the lungs. If the ductus arteriosus remains patent postnatally, the shunt becomes primarily left to right (aorta to pulmonary artery) as PVR falls in normal fashion, resulting in left atrial and LV volume overload. An important exception to this pattern of left heart volume overload occurs in neonates with persistent transitional circulation where the PVR is comparable to or higher than the SVR, resulting in bidirectional shunting through the PDA. If PVR is significantly higher than SVR, the shunting becomes exclusively right to left (pulmonary artery to aorta), causing systemic oxygen desaturations.

The mechanisms responsible for postnatal ductal closure are not fully understood. The ductus arteriosus is highly sensitive to changes in oxygen tension, so the normal postnatal increase in arterial oxygen tension may serve as the stimulus for ductal closure. The mediation of this response is less certain and is likely attributable to a complex interaction among autonomic chemical mediators, prostaglandins, and the ductal musculature. The ductus arteriosus functionally closes in most full-term infants during the first 24 hours of life, but anatomic obliteration of the ductus arteriosus generally does not occur until after the first week of life. A persistent PDA is uncommon in otherwise normal children. In contrast, 30% of infants with birth weight less than 1.5 kg have a PDA, possibly as a result of hypoxia and immaturity of the ductal closure mechanisms, and spontaneous PDA closure by the fourth postnatal day only occurs in approximately one-third of infants weighing less than 1000 g.68 Therefore a majority of very premature infants with hemodynamically significant PDA are potential candidates for pharmacologic, transcatheter, or surgical intervention, although the indications for these interventions remain controversial.

### Associated Defects

A PDA is present at birth in newborns with all but a few congenital heart defects. Although the presenting features of the associated defects are usually clear, occasionally the PDA is the most easily recognized component clinically and by echocardiography. Aortic coarctation in particular can be difficult to definitively diagnose in the presence of a large PDA. Absence of the ductus arteriosus is notable in some neonates with TOF and pulmonary atresia. In these cases,

the central pulmonary arteries are markedly hypoplastic where the ductus arteriosus would insert, and multiple AP collateral vessels may be present. The ductus arteriosus is also often absent in newborns with the absent pulmonary valve TOF variant in which failure of ductal development or closure at a critical time in cardiogenesis may play a role in the pathogenesis of the pulmonary valve and arterial abnormalities.

### Clinical Presentation

The murmur heard in a neonate with a PDA may be unlike that heard in an older infant or child with a persistent PDA, where the classic continuous (machinery) murmur is present. In newborns and infants, especially in the setting of prematurity, diastolic flow through the PDA may be limited due to persistently elevated PVR, and it is consequently difficult to hear. A systolic murmur of uneven intensity throughout systole may be appreciated at the left upper sternal border, peripheral pulses are usually accentuated or bounding, and pulse pressure is increased in a hemodynamically significant PDA. Even in the absence of a murmur, however, significant left-to-right shunting with resultant increased blood flow may result in a supplemental oxygen requirement or cause ventilator weaning difficulties in infants with existing respiratory failure. Clinical evidence of a hemodynamically significant PDA may lag behind echocardiographic findings.

Full-term infants with a small PDA are followed clinically, and spontaneous ductal closure generally occurs in the first months of life. Isolated moderate or large PDAs may also close spontaneously over time but require longitudinal follow-up, with periodic imaging using echocardiography to monitor for interval changes in the left atrial and LV size and to estimate RV pressure as the result of left-to-right shunting. Conventional surgical closure, videoassisted thoracoscopic surgery,70 and transcatheter occlusion are interventional options for newborns and infants with a moderate to large sized PDA. Newer devices such as specifically designed ductal occluders have led to increased experience with transcatheter interventions with excellent results and minimal complications.71

In premature infants, spontaneous ductal closure is common, but persistent or recurrent symptoms, respiratory distress, or failure exacerbated by excessive pulmonary blood flow may require therapy for ductal closure. The optimal approach to the PDA in preterm infants is still unknown. A proportion of infants will have spontaneous closure over the first week of life. Thus some have advocated for delaying assessment of patency until the end of the first week of life. However, there is concern that prolonged exposure to a large hemodynamically significant PDA may compromise the pulmonary vascular bed and may be associated with an increased risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.72 Progressive increases in ventilator or supplemental oxygen support requirements may also be manifestations of an increasingly hemodynamically significant PDA. Medical management with fluid restriction and diuretics is occasionally effective at improving symptomatology. Indomethacin, a prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor, and ibuprofen, a nonselective cyclooxygenase inhibitor, have both been shown to effectively close persistent PDAs in a large number of premature newborns up to 14 days of age and occasionally as late as 1 month of age. Ibuprofen has been further shown to have fewer renal side effects. Repeated courses of indomethacin or ibuprofen may be effective in infants who do not respond to the first or second course. ### Aortopulmonary Window Anatomy and Pathophysiology

An aortopulmonary (AP) window, as its name implies, is an abnormal connection between the ascending aorta and the main pulmonary artery. It results from failure of the conotruncal ridges to fuse during cardiac development. The defects tend to be large, allowing high-pressure shunting from the systemic to the pulmonary circulation, leading to considerable pulmonary overcirculation. AP window pathophysiology mimics that of a large VSD or PDA with significant left-to-right shunting that increases as the PVR falls.

### Associated Defects

AP windows can be present in conjunction with other cardiac anomalies in approximately half of cases, including other conotruncal defects such as TOF, transposition of the great arteries, and interrupted aortic arch (type A). Additional associated abnormalities include right pulmonary artery origin from the aorta and anomalous coronary artery origin from the pulmonary artery.

### Clinical Presentation

Patients with an AP window are at increased risk of developing early pulmonary overcirculation and associated symptomatology, often in the first weeks of life. On examination, the precordium is hyperactive, second heart sound is usually single, and peripheral pulses are bounding.

### Diagnostic Evaluation

Chest radiography often demonstrates cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings consistent with excessive pulmonary blood flow. Diagnosis is made by echocardiography. The location and size of the AP window are delineated, and special care must be taken to identify an associated PDA or interrupted arch, as well as coronary artery or branch pulmonary artery abnormalities.

### Management and Prognosis

Surgical closure of an AP window is usually done shortly after diagnosis with excellent short- and long-term results.75 Delaying repair risks development of significant pulmonary arterial hypertension, potentially irreversible pulmonary vascular disease, and Eisenmenger syndrome.
